docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Route.get('/blogs', BlogController.index); // (1)!

enum Status { active, draft }

@Dto() // (2)!
class BlogFilter {
  final Status status; // ?status=active, else 422
  const BlogFilter({required this.status});
  static const DtoSchema<BlogFilter> schema =
      $BlogFilterDto; // (3)!
}

class BlogController {
  static Future<List<Blog>> index(
    BlogFilter query, // (4)!
  ) async {
    return Blog()
        .where('status', query.status.name)
        .get(); // (5)!
  }
}
  1. A route points at a static method. No reflection, no controller registry.
  2. @Dto() marks an input class. build_runner generates the checks from the fields and their types.
  3. The generated schema. The same schema feeds the OpenAPI docs.
  4. Ask for the DTO as a parameter. Dox reads the query (or the body), checks it, and gives you a typed object. Bad input gets a 422 before your code runs.
  5. The ORM. The same code runs on Postgres, MySQL and SQLite, through native Rust drivers.

docs.title: Fast backendsin Dart
docs.text:
Write in Dart. Serve with Rust.

Dox is a web backend framework for Dart, like Laravel. Routing, an ORM, migrations, validation, auth and a CLI come in one place. It runs one isolate per CPU core and builds to a small native binary.

Build your first API GitHub

docs.title: How fast
docs.text:
1.5× Bun. 2.3× Go. 7× plain Dart.

A real route: read one row from Postgres and return JSON (GET /db). Requests per second on one CPU core, higher is better.

req/s p99 RAM Doxnative server + driver 85,381fastest 5.7 ms 24 MB BunBun.serve + Bun.sql 57,6141.5× slower 6.1 ms 36 MB Gonet/http + pgx 36,7062.3× slower 14.5 ms 18 MB dart:io+ package:postgres 12,1467× slower 47.6 ms 62 MB

Dox 3.0.0-alpha.3 · Bun 1.4 · Go 1.27 · Dart 3.13 · Postgres 18 · 256 connections · wrk · median of 3 runsAll results

Dox also has the lowest p99 (the slowest 1% of requests). Your code is plain Dart. The speed comes from the Rust HTTP server and the Rust database drivers that Dox uses by default. On 2 cores Dox stays ahead on the database routes. Without a database (GET /json), Bun is faster. See Performance for every route and how to run the benchmark yourself.

You are reading the 3.x docs (alpha)

3.0.0-alpha.4 is a preview. Things can still change before the stable release.

docs.title: Run it in two minutes
docs.text:
You need Dart 3.13 or newer. Nothing else: the starter project uses SQLite, so there is no database to install.

dart pub global activate dox 3.0.0-alpha.4   # install the CLI
dox create my_app                            # download the starter project
cd my_app
dart pub get
cp .env.example .env
dox s                                        # start the server

Open a second terminal and call the first route:

curl localhost:3000/ping

pong

That is a Dox app. Keep going with the tutorial: it adds a model, a database table, validation, login and a Docker image, one short step at a time.

The CLI is not found?

dart pub global activate puts dox in $HOME/.pub-cache/bin. Add that folder to your PATH. See Installation.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Fast by default

    A Rust HTTP server, one isolate per CPU core and streamed bodies. dox build makes one native binary. See Performance.

  • ORM and query builder

    Models, relations, migrations and transactions for Postgres, MySQL/MariaDB and SQLite, with native Rust drivers. See Database.

  • Typed validation

    Write a @Dto class. Dox checks the input and gives your controller a typed object. See Validation.

  • OpenAPI

    OpenAPI 3.1 docs and a Scalar docs page, made from your routes and DTOs. See dox_openapi.

  • File storage

    Local disk and S3 behind one API, with signed URLs. See dox_storage.

  • Cache

    Memory, file and Redis cache with tags and locks. See dox_cache.

  • Real time

    WebSocket or Socket.IO, with Redis for many servers.

  • Security

    JWT authentication, CORS, encryption and hashing.

  • CLI

    Create projects, controllers, models and migrations. Run, build and migrate. See CLI reference.

docs.text:

  • Using an AI assistant? Give it llms-full.txt: all of these docs as one plain text file. llms.txt is the page list.
  • Want to help? Read Contribute.

docs.title: Coming from Laravel
docs.text:
This page is for developers who know Laravel. It shows the Laravel way and the Dox way side by side. The Dox code is real 3.x code. The Laravel code is Laravel 11.

Dox follows the ideas of Laravel: routers, controllers, middleware, an ORM with models and relations, migrations, a CLI. But Dox is Dart. It has static types, no reflection at run time, and it compiles to one native binary.

docs.title: Routing
Controllers
docs.text:
Laravel Dox php artisan make:controller BlogController dox create:controller Blog php artisan make:controller BlogController --resource dox create:controller Blog -r public function show(Request $request, int $id) Future<Blog?> show(DoxRequest req, int id) public function store(StoreBlogRequest $request) Future<Blog> store(CreateBlog body) injected by the service container filled by type: DoxRequest, one @Dto class, path params

Dox fills a parameter by its type, not by its name. Path params go by position. A controller can be a class method, a static method or a plain function.

docs.title: Middleware
Requests and validation
Responses
docs.text: Laravel Dox return 'pong'; return 'pong'; return ['a' => 1]; return <String, int>{'a': 1}; return $blog; (JSON) return blog; (JSON from toJson()) return response($data, 201)->header('X-A', 'b'); return response(data).statusCode(201).header('X-A', 'b'); return response()->json($data); return data; (a Map or List is JSON) return response()->file($path); return File(path); return response()->download($path); return Storage().download(path); ->cookie('theme', 'dark') .cookie(DoxCookie('theme', 'dark')) abort(404, 'Not found'); throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'Not found'); new BlogResource($blog) BlogSerializer(blog)

docs.title: Eloquent vs Dox Model
Query builder
docs.text:
Laravel Dox DB::table('users')->get() await QueryBuilder.table('users').get() ->where('a', 1)->orWhere('b', 2) .where('a', 1).orWhere('b', 2) ->whereIn('id', [1, 2]) .whereIn('id', <int>[1, 2]) ->whereNull('deleted_at') .whereNull('deleted_at') ->whereRaw('lower(name) = ?', [$n]) .whereRaw('lower(name) = @n', <String, dynamic>{'n': n}) ->select('id', 'name') .select(<String>['id', 'name']) ->orderBy('name', 'desc')->limit(10)->offset(20) .orderBy('name', 'desc').limit(10).offset(20) ->join('posts', 'posts.user_id', '=', 'users.id') .join('posts', 'posts.user_id', 'users.id') ->groupBy('age') .groupBy('age') (returns maps) ->count() await ....count() ->paginate(10) .paginate(currentPage: 1, perPage: 10) ->insert([...]) .insertMultiple(<Map<String, dynamic>>[...]) ->update([...]) .update(<String, dynamic>{...}) ->delete() .delete() DB::select('select ...', [$id]) QueryBuilder.query('select ... @id', substitutionValues: {'id': id}) DB::transaction(fn) QueryBuilder.transaction(() async { ... }) ->toSql() .toSql() DB::connection('mysql') .withConnection('mysql')

Values are always bound parameters. Names you pass are quoted. Do not pass user input as a column name or an operator.

docs.title: Migrations and schema
Artisan vs the dox CLI
docs.text:
Laravel Dox laravel new blog dox create blog php artisan serve dox serve (or dox s), with hot restart and build_runner watch php artisan make:controller dox create:controller php artisan make:model Blog -m dox create:model Blog -m php artisan make:request dox create:dto php artisan make:middleware dox create:middleware php artisan make:resource dox create:serializer php artisan make:migration dox make:migration php artisan migrate dox migrate php artisan key:generate dox key:generate php artisan route:list not there. Use the OpenAPI docs page at /docs. php artisan tinker not there php artisan optimize dox build (one native binary in build/bundle)

Two commands have no Laravel twin: dox build_runner:build makes the generated code, and dox env:generate makes the typed env class. See Dox CLI.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/auth.php guards and providers Auth.initialize(AuthConfig(guards: ...)) in a service Auth::attempt(['email' => $e, 'password' => $p]) await Auth().attempt(<String, dynamic>{'email': e, 'password': p}) gives a JWT, or null Auth::login($user) Auth().login(user) gives a JWT Auth::user() req.auth?.user<User>() ->middleware('auth:sanctum') AuthMiddleware() from dox_auth Hash::make($p), Hash::check($p, $hash) Hash.make(p), Hash.verify(p, hash)

Dox auth is a JWT in the Authorization header. There are no sessions, no cookies and no Sanctum tokens table. See Authentication.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/cache.php lib/config/cache.dart, CacheConfig(defaultStore:, stores:) Cache::put('k', $v, 600) await Cache().put('k', v, duration: Duration(minutes: 10)) Cache::get('k', 'default') await Cache().get('k', 'default') Cache::remember('k', 600, fn) await Cache().remember('k', Duration(minutes: 10), fn) Cache::forget('k') await Cache().forget('k') Cache::store('redis') Cache().store('redis') Cache::tags(['a']) Cache().tags(<String>['a']) Cache::lock('k', 10) Cache().lock('k', Duration(seconds: 10)) drivers: file, redis, memcached, database, array drivers: file, redis, memory, null

A value must be a JSON type. The memory store is per isolate. See Cache.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/filesystems.php disks lib/config/storage.dart, StorageConfig(defaultDisk:, disks:) Storage::put('a.txt', $bytes) await Storage().put('files', bytes, extension: 'txt') (a uuid file name) $request->file('f')->store('avatars') await file.store('avatars') or Storage().putRequestFile('avatars', file) Storage::get($path) await Storage().get(path) Storage::exists($path) await Storage().exists(path) Storage::delete($path) await Storage().delete(path) Storage::url($path) await Storage().url(path) Storage::temporaryUrl($path, now()->addMinutes(10)) await Storage().signedUrl(path, expiresIn: Duration(minutes: 10)) Storage::disk('s3') Storage().disk('s3') Storage::download($path) return Storage().download(path); drivers: local, s3, ftp, sftp drivers: local, s3 (also R2, MinIO, Spaces), memory

See File Storage.

docs.title: Config and .env
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/*.php files lib/config/*.dart files, put together in AppConfig env('APP_KEY') env.appKey (a getter in lib/config/env.dart) env('APP_PORT', 3000) env.appPort (the default is in the getter: int get appPort => 3000;) config('app.name') env.appName from the typed env class (@DoxEnv()) php artisan config:cache not needed. The typed env is read once, at start.

The typed env class gives you an int for APP_PORT and a build error for a bad type. A missing key stops the app at start, with a list of every missing key. See Environment Variables.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Laravel Dox php artisan test dart test $this->get('/api/ping')->assertStatus(200) start the server once, then http.get(Uri.parse('$baseUrl/api/ping')) RefreshDatabase run the migrations in setUpAll, or use SQLite :memory: Storage::fake('s3') Dox().storage.fake('s3') Cache::fake() Dox().cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(...)) with a memory store $this->actingAs($user) send the JWT from Auth().login(user) in the Authorization header

Dox has no fake HTTP kernel. A test starts the real server with Dox().totalIsolate(1) and sends real requests. See Testing.

docs.title: What is different
docs.text:
• No service container in the controller. Laravel makes your controllers and injects what the constructor asks for. In Dox you make the controller yourself (BlogController()) and pass what it needs. Dox fills only the method parameters: the request, one DTO and the path params. Dox().ioc is a small registry (register, registerSingleton, get), but nothing is injected for you.
  • Isolates, not PHP-FPM workers. One process runs one isolate per CPU core. Each isolate runs your whole app and has its own memory. A static value or a singleton lives once per isolate. A PHP worker starts from zero on each request. A Dox isolate keeps its state between requests, so a memory leak stays. Anything that must be shared goes to the database, Redis or files. See How Dox works.
  • Code generation, not reflection. Laravel reads your classes at run time. Dart has no usable reflection in a compiled app. So build_runner with dox_builder writes the model code, the DTO checks, the env class and the OpenAPI docs into .g.dart files. Run dox build_runner:build after a change, or let dox serve watch for you.
  • One native binary. dox build makes an AOT binary in build/bundle. There is no interpreter, no vendor/ folder and no composer install on the server. The Docker image is about 11 MB.
  • A native HTTP server and native database drivers. Rust parses HTTP and talks to Postgres and MySQL. Your code stays in Dart. The HTTP server comes ready-built. The database drivers need Rust (cargo) to build; without it, Dox uses the Dart drivers.
  • Types everywhere. A DTO is a class with typed fields. A path param is an int. A model field is a String?. The compiler finds many mistakes before you run the app.
  • Async is explicit. Database calls return a Future. You write await. One isolate serves many requests at the same time while it waits for the database.
  • JSON API first. Dox returns text, JSON, files and streams. It has no view layer.

docs.title: What is missing today
docs.text:
Dox 3.0 does not have these Laravel features. Check the packages list for what is there.

Laravel Dox 3.0 Queues and jobs (dispatch(new Job)) not there. Use a database table, Redis or a separate worker process. Task scheduler (schedule()->daily()) not there. Use cron or systemd timers to call a route or a Dart script. Events and listeners (Event::dispatch, $listen) not there. Model events (hooks and observers) are there. Blade views, view() not there. Dox is for APIs. Serve a front end from a CDN or a proxy. Mail (Mail::to()) not there. Use a Dart mail package or an HTTP mail API. Notifications not there Sessions and session cookies not there. Auth uses a JWT. Encrypted cookies are there. Policies and gates not there. Check the user in a middleware or in the controller. Global scopes, $casts, $fillable not there. See Eloquent vs Dox Model. Database seeders and factories not there. Write a Dart script, or a migration with data. Rate limiting middleware not there. Write a middleware with the cache, or use a proxy. php artisan route:list, tinker not there Savepoints in nested transactions not there. A nested transaction() joins the outer one. WebSocket on the native server not there yet. An app with WebSocket routes uses the dart:io server.

What is there, as separate packages: validation, OpenAPI docs, storage, cache, Socket.IO, WebSocket and auth.

docs.title: Dox and the other Dart backends
docs.text:
This page compares Dox with four other ways to build a backend in Dart: Dart Frog, Serverpod, Shelf (with shelf_router) and Alfred. It lists facts only. Each project is good at different things.

Checked on 2026-10-22

The facts about the other projects come from their own docs, READMEs and pub.dev pages, read on 2026-10-22. Projects change. Check their docs before you decide. Where this page is not sure, the table says "see their docs".

docs.title: What each one is for
docs.text:
• Dox is a full backend framework, in the style of Laravel. It has routes, controllers, typed DTOs, an ORM, migrations, auth, cache, storage and a CLI. It is in 3.0 alpha. The API can still change.
  • Dart Frog is a small backend framework. It is built on Shelf. Routes come from the files in the routes/ folder. It describes itself as "a fast, minimalistic backend framework for Dart".
  • Serverpod is a full-stack framework for Flutter. You write endpoint methods on the server. Serverpod generates a typed Dart client for the Flutter app. It has an ORM, auth, streaming and a hosted service (Serverpod Cloud).
  • Shelf is the request and middleware model from the Dart team. It is a library, not a framework. shelf_router adds a router. You pick every other part yourself.
  • Alfred is a small server in the style of Express.js. Routes, middleware, WebSocket and static files are built in.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: This page does not compare speed. Dox's own numbers (hello world and a /db read) are on Performance. To compare, run the same test on your own machine, with each server on the same number of cores.

docs.title: When to pick Dox
docs.text:
• You want a full framework in one place: routes, typed input, ORM, migrations, auth, cache, storage and OpenAPI docs.
  • You know Laravel. See Coming from Laravel.
  • You need MySQL or MariaDB, not only Postgres.
  • You want typed DTOs with the same rules on the server and in a Dart or Flutter client. See Share code with Flutter.
  • You want an OpenAPI document made from your code, for clients that are not written in Dart.
  • You can accept an alpha: the API can change before 3.0 is stable. See Status and roadmap.

docs.title: When to pick something else
docs.text:
• You need a stable API today. Dox is alpha. Dart Frog, Serverpod and Shelf have had 1.0 or later for years.
  • You want a hosted service. Serverpod has Serverpod Cloud. Dox has no hosted service. You deploy it yourself (a binary or Docker).
  • Your app is Flutter only, and you want the client made for you. Serverpod generates a typed client for every endpoint. Dox does not generate a Dart client. It generates an OpenAPI document.
  • You want a small tool with few parts. Dart Frog is simpler. You add only what you need.
  • You want to build your own stack. Shelf gives you the base parts, and the Dart team publishes it.
  • You need features Dox does not have yet, like queues, a scheduler or mail. See What Dox does not have yet.

docs.title: How Dox works
docs.text: This page explains what happens inside Dox when a request comes in. It also explains how Dox uses isolates, where the database pools live, and what each folder of an app is for.

docs.title: The life of a request
docs.text:
Dox has two parts:

  • A native server, written in Rust (dox_http_native). It owns the sockets and parses HTTP.
  • Your app, written in Dart. Routes, middleware, DTOs, controllers and the ORM all run here.

A request goes through these steps:

  1. Rust accepts the connection and reads the request. It parses the HTTP request line, the headers and the body. A bad request gets 400. Headers over 16 KB get 431. A body over the size limit gets 413. Dart never sees these requests.
  2. Rust hands the requests to Dart in a batch. One message holds many requests.
  3. Dart finds the route. It matches the method, the Host (for domain routes) and the path. A plain path is a map lookup. A path with {params} is a pattern match. No match gives 404. A CORS preflight (OPTIONS) gets 204.
  4. Dart adds the CORS headers of the route.
  5. Dart reads the body, only when the request has a Content-Type. A request without a body skips this step.
  6. Dart runs the middleware list of the route, in this order: global middleware, router middleware, group middleware, route middleware. A middleware returns the request to go on. Anything else is sent as the response, and the controller does not run.
  7. Dart fills the controller parameters. Path params are converted first. A value that does not fit its type (abc for int id) gets 404. Then the DTO is read and checked. Bad input gets 422. A body that is not JSON gets 400. A content type Dox can not read gets 415.
  8. The controller runs and returns a value.
  9. The responseHandler from AppConfig runs, when you set one. It can change every response.
  10. Dox turns the value into the response: a String is text, a Map or model is JSON, a File is streamed.
  11. Dart sends the answers of the batch back to Rust in one call. Rust writes the bytes to the socket.

When a step throws, Dox catches the error. An IHttpException (like NotFoundHttpException) gives its own status. Any other error gives 500 and goes to the errorHandler of AppConfig.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant R as Rust (dox_http_native)
    participant D as Dart isolate
    participant M as Middleware
    participant K as Controller

    C->>R: TCP connection, HTTP request
    R->>R: parse request, check size limits
    R->>D: batch of requests (one message)
    D->>D: router: method, host, path
    D->>D: CORS headers, read body
    D->>M: global, router, group, route middleware
    M-->>D: request (go on) or a response
    D->>D: path params, DTO check
    D->>K: call with typed parameters
    K-->>D: return value
    D->>D: responseHandler, build the response
    D->>R: batch of answers (one call)
    R->>C: bytes

No reflection

Dox reads the parameter types of every controller once, at start. It does not use dart:mirrors. DTOs come from a generated list (lib/dtos.g.dart). This is why dox build can make a native (AOT) binary.

docs.title: Where things are decided
docs.text:
Step Code What it decides Route match lib/routes/*.dart, Route.get(...) which controller runs Middleware AppConfig(globalMiddleware:), Router.middleware, Route.middleware(...), the route list go on, or answer early Input a @Dto class in lib/app/http/dtos/ what the controller gets, or 422 Output the return value, response(...), responseHandler status, headers, body Errors IHttpException, AppConfig(errorHandler:) the error response, logging

See Routing, Middleware, Validation and Response.

docs.title: Isolates
docs.text: Dart runs code on isolates. An isolate is like a thread, but it has its own memory. Dox starts one isolate per CPU core (Platform.numberOfProcessors). Every isolate runs the full app.

docs.title: One port, many isolates
docs.text:
Every isolate runs its own HTTP server on the same port. The operating system spreads the connections.

System Native server dart:io server Linux one socket per isolate (SO_REUSEPORT) HttpServer.bind(..., shared: true) macOS the isolates share one socket HttpServer.bind(..., shared: true) Windows only one isolate serves HTTP HttpServer.bind(..., shared: true)

Each isolate also has its own Rust network thread. DOX_HTTP_THREAD=shared puts all isolates on one thread. Leave it off unless you measure a gain.

docs.title: What each isolate gets
docs.text:
Before it starts an isolate, Dox copies three things to it:

  • the AppConfig,
  • the list of services,
  • the routes you added before startServer().

Then each isolate does this, once:

  1. It runs setup() of every service, in list order. This is where a database pool is opened.
  2. It registers the routes of your routers.
  3. It reads the parameter types of every controller.
  4. It starts its HTTP server.

Nothing in this list runs per request.

Because the config and the services are copied, they must not hold open sockets or pools. Open these in setup(). See Services.

docs.title: Each isolate has its own memory
docs.text:
• A static value or a singleton exists once per isolate. A change in one isolate is not seen in the others.
  • The memory cache store is per isolate. Use the redis store to share cache data.
  • To share data between isolates, use the database, Redis or files.
  • Dox().isolateId tells you which isolate runs the code. The first one is 1.

docs.title: When an isolate crashes
docs.text:
• An error in a request is caught. Dox answers 500 and keeps going.
  • An async error outside a request is caught and passed to errorHandler. The isolate keeps running.
  • When a worker isolate still dies, Dox prints [dox] isolate N exited, restarting and starts a new one after 1 second.
  • When the first (main) isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. A supervisor (Docker restart:, systemd Restart=always) must start it again.

docs.title: How many isolates
docs.text: Set totalIsolate in AppConfig, or APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE in .env. In code, Dox().totalIsolate(2) before startServer() wins over the config. Use 1 in tests. See Isolate.

docs.title: Where the database pools live
docs.text:
The ORM is started in a service (ORMService). Every isolate runs setup(), so every isolate opens its own pool.

Driver Per isolate Per process Postgres native (dox_postgres_native) one pool of maxConnectionCount connections one Rust runtime, shared by all pools (extra['threads'], default 1) MySQL native (dox_mysql_native) one pool one Rust runtime, shared by all pools Dart drivers (postgres, mysql_dart) one pool nothing shared SQLite one connection nothing shared

So the total number of connections is isolates × maxConnectionCount. With 8 cores and the default of 10, the app can open 80 connections. Set maxConnectionCount with this in mind.

Share one native pool between isolates

A native pool has a handle (an int). Give it to another isolate and use PostgresNativeDriver(PgNativePool.fromHandle(handle)) there. Then both isolates use one pool. See Native Postgres driver.

The native drivers are the default. When the native library does not load, the ORM uses the Dart driver and prints one warning line. Set DOX_DB_DRIVER=dart to use the Dart drivers on purpose. See Database.

docs.title: The layout of a Dox app
docs.text:
dox create my_app copies the dox-sample template. It looks like this:

my_app/
├── bin/
│   └── server.dart          # starts the app
├── db/
│   └── migration/           # migrations (.dart with a registry, or .sql)
├── lib/
│   ├── app/
│   │   ├── http/
│   │   │   ├── controllers/     # *.controller.dart
│   │   │   ├── dtos/            # *.dto.dart, typed and checked input
│   │   │   ├── middleware/      # *.middleware.dart
│   │   │   ├── serializers/     # *.serializer.dart, custom JSON shapes
│   │   │   └── response_handler.dart
│   │   ├── models/              # one folder per model, *.model.dart
│   │   └── ws/controllers/      # WebSocket controllers (dox_websocket)
│   ├── config/
│   │   ├── app.dart             # AppConfig: port, isolates, routers, middleware
│   │   ├── cache.dart           # cache stores
│   │   ├── cors.dart
│   │   ├── database.dart        # DatabaseConfig: connections
│   │   ├── env.dart             # typed env class (@DoxEnv), optional
│   │   ├── logger.dart
│   │   ├── services.dart        # the list of DoxService
│   │   └── storage.dart         # storage disks
│   ├── routes/
│   │   ├── api.dart             # ApiRouter, prefix `api`
│   │   └── web.dart             # WebRouter
│   ├── services/
│   │   └── orm_service.dart     # opens the database in every isolate
│   ├── dtos.g.dart              # generated: the list of DTOs
│   └── openapi.g.dart           # generated: the OpenAPI docs
├── storage/                     # local disk, file cache, uploads
├── test/
├── .env                         # local settings, not in git
├── .env.example
├── Dockerfile
├── docker-compose.yml
└── pubspec.yaml
Folder What goes there bin/ server.dart calls Dox().initialize(appConfig), runs the migrations, then Dox().startServer(). dox make:migration adds migrate.dart. db/migration/ Your migrations. Dart migrations are listed in migrations.dart, which the CLI writes. lib/app/http/ Everything about HTTP: controllers, DTOs, middleware, serializers. lib/app/models/ One folder per model. build_runner writes the .g.dart file next to it. lib/config/ One file per config object. app.dart puts them together in AppConfig. lib/routes/ One Router class per file. Add each router to routers in app.dart. lib/services/ Classes that implement DoxService. Their setup() runs in every isolate. lib/*.g.dart Generated files. Do not edit them. Run dox build_runner:build to make them again. storage/ Files the app writes: uploads, the file cache, SQLite files.

Generated code comes from build_runner with the dox_builder package. It makes the model classes, the DTO checks, the typed env class and the OpenAPI docs. Run dox build_runner:build after you change a model, a DTO or the env class. dox serve runs it in watch mode for you.

docs.title: Status and roadmap
docs.text:
Checked on 2026-10-22, for version 3.0.0-alpha.4.

Dox 3.0 is an alpha. You can build with it, but the API can still change between alpha versions. All packages share one version number.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
What the states mean:

  • May change: works and has tests. Names and options can still change before 3.0 is stable.
  • Experimental: new code. It changed in a breaking way during the alphas, or it has a known gap.

No package is marked "stable API" yet. That comes with 3.0 stable.

Package What it does State Tests dox_core Routes, middleware, controllers, request and response, isolates, config May change 29 test files. CI runs them on the native server and on dart:io. dox_orm Query builder, models, relations, transactions, drivers May change 16 test files. CI runs them on Postgres, MariaDB, MySQL 8.4 and SQLite, with the native and the Dart drivers. dox_validation @Dto rules, fluent schemas, JSON Schema, Standard Schema May change 6 test files dox_builder Code generator for models, DTOs, env classes and OpenAPI May change 4 test files dox_annotation Annotations used by the generator May change 1 small test file. Mostly tested through dox_builder. dox (CLI) dox create, dox serve, dox build, make:*, migration:* May change 5 test files dox_migration Migrations for Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite May change 2 test files. CI runs them on each database. dox_auth JWT auth guard and middleware, password hashing May change 2 test files dox_cache Memory, file and Redis cache, tags, locks May change 4 test files, with Redis in CI dox_storage Local disk and S3 (and S3-compatible) storage May change 7 test files, with MinIO in CI dox_openapi OpenAPI 3.1 document and a docs page May change 4 test files dox_websocket WebSocket routes and events May change 4 test files, with Redis in CI dox_socketio Socket.IO v4 server with a Redis adapter May change 6 test files, with the real socket.io-client in CI dox_http_native Native HTTP/1.1 server (Rust hyper), the default server Experimental 2 Dart test files and Rust tests. No WebSocket yet. Big responses are held in memory. dox_postgres_native Native Postgres client (Rust tokio-postgres), the default Postgres driver Experimental 1 Dart test file, plus the dox_orm tests. No TLS yet. dox_mysql_native Native MySQL and MariaDB client (Rust mysql_async), the default MySQL driver Experimental 1 Dart test file, plus the dox_orm tests

About test coverage

The repo does not measure line coverage. The "Tests" column counts test files and says where CI runs them. The CI setup is in .github/workflows/test.yaml and native.yaml.

docs.title: What Dox does not have yet
docs.text:
These were checked by searching the code in packages/*/lib with rg.

Feature Status What to do today Queues and jobs Not there Use a database table, Redis or a separate worker process. See Background work. Task scheduler Not there Use cron or a systemd timer to call a route or a Dart script. Mail Not there Use a Dart mail package or an HTTP mail API. Events and listeners Not there Model events are there. See Model events. Views and templates Not there Dox is for APIs. Serve the front end on its own. Rate limiting Not there Write a middleware with the cache, or use a proxy. Sessions Not there Auth uses JWT. On the native server, req.httpRequest.session throws UnsupportedError. Policies and gates Not there Check the user in a middleware or in the controller. Database seeders Not there Write a Dart script, or a migration with data.

docs.title: Planned
docs.text:
This is a plan, not a promise. Open an issue to discuss.

Items come from the code (TODO and ponytail: notes in packages/*/lib) and from the owner. There are no dates.

Today a big file is held in memory. ponytail: note in dox_http_native/lib/src/response.dart TLS for the native Postgres driver ponytail: note in dox_orm/lib/src/drivers/postgres_native_driver.dart Savepoints for nested transactions. Today a nested transaction() joins the outer one. ponytail: notes in the dox_orm drivers and in dox_migration A queue package (dox_queue) Wanted by the owner. Not started. A mail package (dox_mail) Wanted by the owner. Not started. 3.0 stable After the alpha API settles

The package CHANGELOGs have no Unreleased section today. When one is added, it lists the next changes.

docs.title: How to help
docs.text:
• Try the alpha and open an issue when something breaks or is missing.
  • Pick an item above and open an issue first, so the design can be discussed.
  • See Contribute to set up the repo and run the tests.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
This page shows how to connect Dox to a database. Dox works with Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite through the dox_orm package.

  • Query builder: build SQL with methods.
  • Models: one class per table.
  • Transactions: many queries that succeed or fail together.
  • Migration and Schema: create and change tables.

This is how a query travels from your code to the database:

flowchart LR
    M["Model or QueryBuilder"] --> S["SQL text<br>quoted names, @values"]
    S --> D{"Driver"}
    D --> N["Native Rust pool<br>dox_postgres_native, dox_mysql_native"]
    D --> T["Dart driver<br>postgres, mysql_dart, sqlite3"]
    N --> DB[("Database")]
    T --> DB

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The query builder and the models are in the dox_orm package.

dart pub add dox_orm

import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

docs.title: Supported databases
Config
docs.text:
Put the connections in lib/config/database.dart. connection is the name of the default connection.

lib/config/database.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: 'localhost',
      port: 5432,
      user: 'postgres',
      password: 'postgres',
      database: 'postgres',
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: false,
    ),
    'mysql': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.mysql, // also for MariaDB
      host: 'localhost',
      port: 3306,
      user: 'root',
      password: 'password',
      database: 'dox',
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: false,
    ),
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: 'storage/app.db', // file path, or ':memory:'
      debug: false,
    ),
  },
);
  • debug: true prints each SQL query and its values.
  • user, password, host and port are not used by SQLite.

Start the ORM in a service. Each isolate runs the service, so each isolate gets its own pool.

lib/services/orm_service.dart
class ORMService implements DoxService {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }
}

docs.title: .env
docs.text:
The app config and the migration commands read these values.

.env
DB_CONNECTION=postgres # postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432           # 3306 for mysql
DB_NAME=dox            # for sqlite: the file path, like storage/app.db
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=postgres

docs.title: extra options
docs.text:
extra is a map in ConnectionConfig for driver options.

Key Database Default What it does maxConnectionCount Postgres, MySQL 10 Most connections in the pool. native Postgres, MySQL true false uses the Dart driver for this connection. threads Postgres, MySQL 1 Rust threads of the native driver. maxConnectionAge MySQL 12 hours A connection older than this is opened again. preparedStatementCacheSize MySQL, and the Dart Postgres and SQLite drivers 100 Prepared statements kept per connection. timeZone Postgres UTC Time zone of the session. applicationName Postgres none Name of the app in pg_stat_activity. busyTimeout SQLite 5000 Milliseconds a query waits for a lock.

The Dart drivers read some more keys. The Dart Postgres driver reads the PoolSettings keys of the postgres package, like sslMode, queryTimeout and connectTimeout. The Dart MySQL driver reads collation (default utf8mb4_general_ci), timeoutMs, timeZone, serverPublicKey and allowPublicKeyRetrieval.

MySQL 8 login without TLS

The MySQL 8 default login (caching_sha2_password) works without TLS. The Dart driver then asks the server for its RSA key to encrypt the password. To not ask, give the key in serverPublicKey, or set useSSL: true. Set allowPublicKeyRetrieval: false to turn the asking off.

docs.title: Table and column names are quoted
docs.text:
Table and column names you pass to select, where, join, groupBy, orderBy, insert and update are quoted. Postgres and SQLite use "name". MySQL uses `name`. So names like order or key work.

  • table.column, * and column as alias are quoted in the right way.
  • A value with ( (for example count(*) as total) is kept as it is.
  • For anything else, use the raw methods (selectRaw, whereRaw, joinRaw).
  • On Postgres, a quoted name is case sensitive. userId is not the same column as userid.

docs.title: Raw queries
docs.text:
QueryBuilder.query() runs SQL on the default connection. Use @name for values. The values are sent as bound parameters.

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.query(
  'select * from blog where id = @id',
  substitutionValues: <String, dynamic>{'id': 1},
);

docs.title: Other connections
docs.text:
Use withConnection() with a connection name from the config.

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('blog')
    .withConnection('mysql')
    .get();

docs.title: MySQL and MariaDB
docs.text:
• The default driver is dox_mysql_native. The fallback Dart driver is mysql_dart.
  • Both have a connection pool and send values as bound parameters.
  • MySQL 8 and 9 login (caching_sha2_password) works.
  • CREATE, ALTER and DROP are saved right away. A transaction can not undo them.

MySQL values are converted by column type:

MySQL / MariaDB Dart Integer types int FLOAT, DOUBLE, DECIMAL double DATE, DATETIME, TIMESTAMP DateTime, read as UTC boolean() columns (TINYINT(1)) bool TIME String JSON Map or List

JSON on MariaDB

MariaDB stores JSON as LONGTEXT, so the driver can not see the column type. On MariaDB, text that starts with { or [ and is valid JSON is decoded. Other text columns are not decoded.

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text:
SQLite is good for development, tests and small apps. For a busy production app, use Postgres or MySQL.

How it runs

The sqlite3 package calls SQLite directly (FFI). A query blocks the isolate while it runs. Each isolate has one connection. While a transaction is open, the other queries of that isolate wait. The database file uses WAL mode, so readers do not wait for the writer. busy_timeout makes a query wait for a lock from another isolate, instead of failing. Foreign keys are turned on.

Types

SQLite has no bool, JSON or date type. Dox converts them for you:

  • boolean() is saved as 0/1 and read back as bool.
  • json() is saved as text and read back as Map or List.
  • Dates are saved as ISO text in UTC and read back as DateTime.

The driver uses the column type in CREATE TABLE. It finds the table by the table names in the query. So it works on tables made by Schema, or by SQL with the same type names (BOOLEAN, JSON, TIMESTAMP, DATE, DATETIME). A column with an alias (active as is_active) is not converted.

Limits

  • schema.table with .change() makes the table again and copies the rows. See SQLite notes.
  • dropColumn does not work on a primary key, unique or indexed column.
  • A new column with NOT NULL needs a default value.
  • truncate() runs DELETE FROM and resets the id counter.
  • insertMultiple with rows that have different keys inserts the rows one by one, because SQLite has no DEFAULT in VALUES.
  • SQLite before 3.39 has no RIGHT JOIN.

Native library

The sqlite3 package (v3) bundles SQLite with a build hook. You do not install a system library. dart run and dart test run the hook by themselves. For the AOT binary, use dox build (it runs dart build cli). It puts the library in build/bundle/lib/, next to build/bundle/bin/server. Keep the two folders together. dart compile exe does not work with build hooks. See Deployment.

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
A migration changes your database schema step by step: create a table, add a column, and so on. Each migration has an up method (make the change) and a down method (undo it).

Write migrations in Dart with the schema builder. The same migration then works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. Plain .sql migrations still work too.

docs.title: Create a migration
docs.text:
dox make:migration create_users_table

This makes db/migration/2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart. The numbers are the date and time when you run the command.

db/migration/2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class CreateUsersTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('users', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('users');
  }
}

Add your columns in up, for example table.string('email').unique();. See Schema for all column types.

The name of the migration decides what the new file contains:

Name The file has create_users_table schema.create('users', ...) in up, and dropIfExists('users') in down add_avatar_to_users_table (also _from_, _in_, _on_) schema.table('users', ...) in up and down any other name empty up and down
  • create:migration is the old name of the same command.
  • dox create:model Blog -m makes the model and a create_blogs_table migration.

Raw SQL and data in a Dart migration

schema.driver runs raw SQL on the same connection and transaction: await schema.driver.execute("UPDATE users SET role = 'admin' WHERE id = 1"); Do not use models or QueryBuilder in a migration. They use another connection.

docs.title: The registry
docs.text:
Dart can not load a file at run time in an AOT build. So Dox keeps a list of your Dart migrations in db/migration/migrations.dart:

// Made by `dox make:migration` and the `dox migration:*` commands.
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart' as m1;

final List<MigrationEntry> migrations = <MigrationEntry>[
  MigrationEntry(
    '2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table',
    m1.CreateUsersTable(),
  ),
];
  • dox make:migration and every dox migration:* command write this file again. You do not edit it.
  • It finds each file named YYYY_MM_DD_HHMMSS_name.dart and its class ... extends Migration.
  • The name of a migration is its file name without .dart. The order is by name.

The first dox make:migration also makes bin/migrate.dart in your app:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await Migrator(migrations: migrations).run(args);
}

The dox migration:* commands run dart run bin/migrate.dart <command>. So your migrations run as part of your app code.

docs.title: Run migrations
docs.text:
Command What it does dox migration:run Run the migrations that did not run yet. Short name: dox migrate. dox migration:rollback Undo the last batch. dox migration:rollback --step=2 Undo the last 2 migrations, even across batches. dox migration:reset Undo all migrations. dox migration:refresh Undo all migrations, then run them again. dox migration:status Show each migration, its batch, and if it ran.

migrate:rollback, migrate:reset, migrate:refresh and migrate:status are short names.

A batch is the group of migrations that ran in one migration:run. Migrations are undone newest first. The ran migrations are saved in the dox_db_migration table.

When a migration fails, the error shows its name, and the command exits with code 1. The failed migration is not saved, and the later ones do not run.

You can also run dart run bin/migrate.dart run (or rollback --step=2, reset, refresh, status) yourself.

docs.title: Run on server start
docs.text:
The AOT server binary can run the migrations, because the registry is compiled in. The new app template already does this:

bin/server.dart
import 'package:dox_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() async {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
  await Migrator(migrations: migrations).migrate();
  await Dox().startServer();
}

Keep the db/migration folder next to the binary if you also have .sql migrations.

docs.title: Database settings
docs.text:
The migrations use the .env file in your project. When there is no .env file (for example in Docker), they use the environment variables.

.env
DB_CONNECTION=postgres # or mysql (also MariaDB), or sqlite
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=postgres
DB_USERNAME=admin
DB_PASSWORD=password

For SQLite, only two variables are needed:

.env
DB_CONNECTION=sqlite
DB_NAME=storage/app.db # file path, made if missing
  • DB_DATABASE works too, in place of DB_NAME.
  • The default port is 5432 for Postgres and 3306 for MySQL.
  • One run uses one database connection.
  • Migrations do not use TLS. To migrate a database that needs TLS, give your own connection: Migrator(migrations: migrations, connection: myPool).

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
Each migration runs in one transaction. On Postgres and SQLite, a failed migration undoes all its changes.

MySQL

On MySQL and MariaDB, CREATE, ALTER and DROP save right away. So if a migration fails half way, these changes stay. Only data changes are undone. Keep each MySQL migration small: one table change per migration.

To run a migration without a transaction (for example CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on Postgres):

class AddSearchIndex extends Migration {
  @override
  bool get withinTransaction => false;

  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.driver.execute(
      'CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY posts_title_index ON posts (title)',
    );
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.driver.execute('DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY posts_title_index');
  }
}

SQLite foreign keys

On SQLite, foreign key checks are off while a migration runs. This lets Dox make a table again (see SQLite notes). Before the end, Dox checks all foreign keys. The migration fails if one is broken.

docs.title: SQL migrations
docs.text:
A .sql migration is still fine. Use it for SQL that only one database understands.

dox make:migration create_blog_table --sql

-- up
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS blog (
    id serial PRIMARY KEY,
    title VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);

-- down
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS blog
  • Put the up SQL under a line -- up, and the down SQL under a line -- down. Each of these lines must be on its own line. Other -- lines are normal SQL comments.
  • Statements are split on ;. A ; inside quotes, comments or a postgres $$ ... $$ body does not split.

SQLite ids

In SQLite, id serial PRIMARY KEY does not make an auto increment id. The id stays NULL. Use id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT for SQLite. table.id() in Dart does this for you.

docs.title: Dart and SQL in one folder
docs.text:
Both kinds can live in db/migration. They run in file name order (the timestamp).

  • With bin/migrate.dart: the Migrator runs the Dart migrations from the registry and reads the .sql files from the folder, merged by name.
  • Without bin/migrate.dart (a project with only .sql files): dox runs the .sql files itself, like before.
  • A Dart and a .sql migration with the same name is an error.

docs.title: Native MySQL driver
docs.text:
dox_mysql_native is the default MySQL and MariaDB driver of the Dox ORM. Rust talks to the database. Your models, queries and transactions stay the same. You do not change any config.

  • Rust (mysql_async) owns the connections and the pool.
  • Dart sends many queries to Rust in one call. Rust sends many results back in one message.
  • Each connection keeps its prepared statements. The same SQL is not prepared again.
  • Values have the same Dart types as with the Dart driver (mysql_dart). Errors are the same MySQLServerException class.
  • Works with MySQL 8.4 (the default caching_sha2_password login) and MariaDB 11.

Alpha

This driver is new. If you see a problem, use the Dart driver and tell us.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
One find-by-id query (SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = @id), AOT build (dart build cli), database on the same machine (Apple M-series), 10 connections, one isolate:

Dart driver Native driver MySQL 8.4, one query at a time 61 µs 67 µs MySQL 8.4, 32 queries in flight 25 µs per query 11 µs per query MySQL 8.4, CPU time of the app per query 32 µs 13.5 µs MariaDB 11, one query at a time 59 µs 63 µs MariaDB 11, 32 queries in flight 25.5 µs per query 9.7 µs per query MariaDB 11, CPU time of the app per query 32.5 µs 12.4 µs

The CPU time counts the Dart thread and the Rust thread. It is the limit on one CPU core: about 31,000 queries per second with the Dart driver and about 75,000 with the native driver.

One query at a time is about the same speed: most of the time is the trip to the database. The gain is big when many requests run at the same time, like in a web server.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
dox_orm depends on dox_mysql_native. You do not add it yourself. Add it only to use MysqlNativePool without the ORM:

dart pub add dox_mysql_native

The build hook builds the Rust library with cargo, so you need Rust installed. Ready-built libraries (like the ones dox_http_native has) are not published for this driver yet. Without Rust, the ORM still works: it uses the Dart driver and prints one warning line (see below).

Use dart run, dart test or dart build cli. dart compile exe does not run build hooks.

docs.title: Native is the default
docs.text:
You do not change any config. The ORM picks the driver like this:

  1. driverFactory is set: the ORM uses your driver. It wins over everything below.
  2. You ask for the Dart driver (see below): the ORM uses the Dart driver.
  3. The native library loads: the ORM uses the native driver.
  4. The native library does not load (no library for your system, no Rust to build it, or a load error): the ORM uses the Dart driver. It prints one warning line to stderr, like this:
[dox] warning: dox_mysql_native did not load, using the Dart mysql driver (...)

Named connections (withConnection('x'), transaction(..., connection: 'x')) follow the same rules.

docs.title: Use the Dart driver
docs.text:
For all connections, set the env var:

DOX_DB_DRIVER=dart dart run bin/server.dart

For one connection, set native: false in extra:

ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.mysql,
  // ... host, user, password, database as before
  extra: <String, dynamic>{'native': false},
  debug: false,
),

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The driver reads the normal fields of the ConnectionConfig (host, port, user, password, database, useSSL) and these keys from extra:

Key Default What it does maxConnectionCount 10 Most connections in the pool. maxConnectionAge 12 hours A connection older than this is closed and opened again. preparedStatementCacheSize 100 Prepared statements kept per connection. threads 1 Rust threads for all pools of the process. Only the first pool sets it. One thread is the fastest for most apps.

Isolates that open a pool with the same settings share one pool in Rust. So maxConnectionCount is for the whole process, not per isolate. You can also give driver.pool.handle (an int) to another isolate and use MysqlNativeDriver(MysqlNativePool.fromHandle(handle)) there. MysqlNativeDriver comes from package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart.

docs.title: Use it without the ORM
docs.text:
MysqlNativePool pool = MysqlNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'root',
  password: 'password',
  database: 'app',
);

MysqlNativeResult result = await pool.query(
  'SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = ?',
  parameters: <Object?>[1],
);
print(result.rows); // [{id: 1, name: Ada}]

MysqlNativeResult insert = await pool.query(
  'INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (@name)',
  parameters: <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Bob'},
);
print(insert.insertId); // the new AUTO_INCREMENT id
print(insert.affectedRows); // 1

int tx = await pool.begin();
await pool.execute('UPDATE users SET name = ?', parameters: <Object?>['Cy'], transaction: tx);
await pool.commit(tx); // or pool.rollback(tx)
  • parameters is a list for ?, or a map for @name.
  • execute is like query, but the rows are not sent back to Dart.
  • A transaction runs on one connection. Its queries run in the order you send them.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
The same as the Dox ORM on the Dart driver:

MySQL / MariaDB Dart TINYINT(1) (boolean()) bool TINYINT, SMALLINT, INT, BIGINT, YEAR int FLOAT, DOUBLE, DECIMAL double CHAR, VARCHAR, TEXT, ENUM String DATE, DATETIME, TIMESTAMP DateTime in UTC TIME String, like 12:34:56 JSON the decoded JSON value BLOB, BINARY, VARBINARY Uint8List NULL null

MariaDB keeps JSON columns as LONGTEXT. So on MariaDB, TEXT that is a JSON object or array comes back decoded. The Dart driver does the same.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A server error throws the same exception as the Dart driver: MySQLServerException, with the same errorCode (eg. 1062 for a duplicate key) and message. Other errors (eg. the server is down) throw MySQLClientException.

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• The timeZone, collation, serverPublicKey and timeoutMs keys of the Dart driver are not read. The connection uses utf8mb4.
  • A login with sha256_password (not the default) does not work. The default caching_sha2_password and mysql_native_password work.
  • A nested transaction() joins the outer one, like the Dart driver (no savepoints).

docs.title: Native Postgres driver
docs.text:
dox_postgres_native is the default Postgres driver of the Dox ORM. Rust talks to the database. Your models, queries and transactions stay the same. You do not change any config.

  • Rust (tokio-postgres) owns the connections and the pool.
  • Dart sends many queries to Rust in one call. Rust sends many results back in one message.
  • Each connection keeps its prepared statements. The same SQL is not parsed again.
  • Values have the same Dart types as with the postgres package. Errors are the same ServerException classes.

Alpha

This driver is new. If you see a problem, use the Dart driver and tell us.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
One find-by-id query (SELECT ... WHERE id = @id), AOT build (dart build cli), Postgres 14 on the same machine (Apple M-series), 4 connections:

Dart driver Native driver One query at a time 95 µs 60 µs 64 queries in flight, one isolate 45 µs per query 12.5 µs per query 4 isolates, 64 in flight each, 16 connections per pool 39,500 queries/s 64,000 queries/s

The gain is biggest when many requests run at the same time, like in a web server.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
dox_orm depends on dox_postgres_native. You do not add it yourself. Add it only to use PgNativePool without the ORM:

dart pub add dox_postgres_native

The build hook builds the Rust library with cargo, so you need Rust installed. Ready-built libraries (like the ones dox_http_native has) are not published for this driver yet. Without Rust, the ORM still works: it uses the Dart driver and prints one warning line (see below).

Use dart run, dart test or dart build cli. dart compile exe does not run build hooks.

docs.title: Native is the default
docs.text:
You do not change any config. The ORM picks the driver like this:

  1. driverFactory is set: the ORM uses your driver. It wins over everything below.
  2. You ask for the Dart driver (see below), or the connection uses TLS: the ORM uses the Dart driver.
  3. The native library loads: the ORM uses the native driver.
  4. The native library does not load (no library for your system, no Rust to build it, or a load error): the ORM uses the Dart driver. It prints one warning line to stderr, like this:
[dox] warning: dox_postgres_native did not load, using the Dart postgres driver (...)

Named connections (withConnection('x'), transaction(..., connection: 'x')) follow the same rules.

docs.title: Use the Dart driver
docs.text:
For all connections, set the env var:

DOX_DB_DRIVER=dart dart run bin/server.dart

For one connection, set native: false in extra:

ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.postgres,
  // ... host, user, password, database as before
  extra: <String, dynamic>{'native': false},
  debug: false,
),

Postgres with TLS (useSSL: true or extra['sslMode']) always uses the Dart driver, because the native driver has no TLS yet.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The driver reads these keys from extra of the ConnectionConfig:

Key Default What it does maxConnectionCount 10 Most connections in the pool. timeZone UTC Time zone of the session, like the Dart driver. applicationName none Name of the app in pg_stat_activity. threads 1 Rust threads for all pools of the process. 0 is one thread with a single-thread runtime. Only the first pool sets it.

Each isolate that runs setup() makes its own pool. To share one pool between isolates, give driver.pool.handle (an int) to the other isolates and use PostgresNativeDriver(PgNativePool.fromHandle(handle)) there. PostgresNativeDriver comes from package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart.

docs.title: Use it without the ORM
docs.text:
PgNativePool pool = PgNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'postgres',
  password: 'postgres',
  database: 'postgres',
);

PgNativeResult result = await pool.query(
  'SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = @id',
  parameters: <String, dynamic>{'id': 1},
);
print(result.rows); // [{id: 1, name: Ada}]

int tx = await pool.begin();
await pool.query('UPDATE users SET name = @n', parameters: <String, dynamic>{'n': 'Bob'}, transaction: tx);
await pool.commit(tx); // or pool.rollback(tx)
  • parameters is a map for @name, or a list for $1, $2.
  • A transaction runs on one connection. Its queries run in the order you send them.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
The same as the postgres package:

Postgres Dart int2, int4, int8 int float4, float8 double numeric String text, varchar, char String bool bool timestamp, timestamptz, date DateTime in UTC json, jsonb the decoded JSON value uuid String bytea Uint8List arrays of most types above List NULL null

Other types decode with the type registry of the postgres package.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A server error throws the same exception as the Dart driver: ServerException, or UniqueViolationException and ForeignKeyViolationException, with the same code, detail, constraintName and other fields. Other errors (eg. the server is down) throw PgException.

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• SSL. A connection with useSSL: true uses the Dart driver.
  • maxConnectionAge, queryTimeout and the other extra keys of the Dart driver are not read.
  • A nested transaction() joins the outer one, like the Dart driver (no savepoints).

docs.title: Query Builder
docs.text:
The query builder makes SQL for you. You chain methods, and Dox runs the query with bound values. It works on Postgres, MySQL/MariaDB and SQLite.

  • Set up the database first. See Database.
  • For transactions, see Transactions.

docs.title: Start a query
docs.text:
There are two ways to start a query.

// with a model: the result is a list of Actor models
List<Actor> actors = await Actor().where('age', '>=', 23).get();

// with a table name: the result is a list of maps, one map per row
List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .where('age', '>=', 23)
    .get();

See Models for the model way.

The examples on this page use an Actor model on the table actor. The SQL in the examples is for Postgres. MySQL quotes names with ` instead of ".

Start each query with a new object

A query object keeps its where, orderBy and other parts. Use Actor() (or QueryBuilder.table(...)) again for each new query.

docs.title: get
docs.text:
Runs the query and returns all rows that match.

List<Actor> actors = await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').get();
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = @name_p0

docs.title: all
docs.text:
Returns all rows of the table. all() ignores where, join, orderBy and limit. Use get() for those.

List<Actor> actors = await Actor().all();
// SELECT * FROM "actor"

docs.title: find
docs.text:
Returns one row, or null when there is no match.

// by primary key
Actor? actor = await Actor().find(1);
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "id" = @id_p0 LIMIT 1

// by another column
Actor? byName = await Actor().find('name', 'John Wick');
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = @name_p0 LIMIT 1

docs.title: getFirst
docs.text:
Returns the first row of the query, or null.

Actor? actor = await Actor().where('age', '>', 60).orderBy('age').getFirst();
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "age" > @age_p0 ORDER BY "age" LIMIT 1

docs.title: count
docs.text:
Returns the number of rows as an int.

int total = await Actor().count();
int adults = await Actor().where('age', '>=', 18).count();
// SELECT count(*) as total FROM "actor" WHERE "age" >= @age_p0
  • count() ignores limit, offset and orderBy.
  • With groupBy, count() returns the number of groups.

docs.title: paginate
docs.text:
Returns one page of rows and the page info. It runs a count() query and a get() query.

Pagination page = await Actor()
    .where('age', '>=', 18)
    .paginate(currentPage: 2, perPage: 10);

List<Actor> actors = page.getData<Actor>();
print(page.total);    // rows that match
print(page.lastPage); // number of pages

page.toJson() gives total, per_page, last_page, current_page and data. So you can return a Pagination from a controller.

docs.title: where
docs.text:
// equal
await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').get();
// WHERE "name" = @name_p0

// other operator
await Actor().where('age', '>=', 23).get();
await Actor().where('name', '!=', 'John Wick').get();
await Actor().where('name', 'like', 'John%').get();

// null
await Actor().where('deleted_at', null).get();
// WHERE "deleted_at" IS NULL

Many where calls are joined with AND.

Warning

The operator is written into the SQL as it is. Do not pass user input as the operator or as the column name.

docs.title: orWhere
docs.text:
await Actor().where('name', 'John Doe').orWhere('name', 'John Wick').get();
// WHERE "name" = @name_p0 OR "name" = @name_p1

await Actor().where('age', '<', 18).orWhere('age', '>', 60).get();

docs.title: whereIn and whereNotIn
docs.text:
await Actor().whereIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
// WHERE "id" IN (@id_p0,@id_p1)

await Actor().whereNotIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereNotIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
  • Each value is sent as a bound parameter.
  • An empty list matches no rows for whereIn, and all rows for whereNotIn.

docs.title: whereNull and whereNotNull
docs.text:
await Actor().whereNull('deleted_at').get();
await Actor().whereNotNull('deleted_at').get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereNull('deleted_at').get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereNotNull('deleted_at').get();

docs.title: whereRaw and orWhereRaw
docs.text:
Write the condition yourself. Put values in a map, and use @key in the SQL. The column names are not quoted.

await Actor().whereRaw('name = @name', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick'}).get();

await Actor()
    .where('age', 60)
    .orWhereRaw('lower(name) = @name', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'john wick'})
    .get();

Warning

Never put user input into the SQL text. Always send it in the map.

docs.title: Select
docs.text:
select sets the columns. Each call replaces the columns of the call before.

// a list
await Actor().select(<String>['id', 'name']).get();
// SELECT "id","name" FROM "actor"

// comma separated
await Actor().select('id, name, age').get();

// with a function
await Actor().select('count(*) as total, name').groupBy('name').get();
// SELECT count(*) as total,"name" FROM "actor" GROUP BY "name"

// raw: nothing is quoted
await Actor().selectRaw('DISTINCT name').get();

A part with ( is kept as it is. Other parts are quoted.

Info

A model loaded with select() only has the selected fields. save() on it only updates the fields it has.

docs.title: orderBy
docs.text:
await Actor().orderBy('name').get();
await Actor().orderBy('name', 'desc').get();
await Actor().orderBy('name', 'asc').orderBy('id', 'desc').get();
// ORDER BY "name" asc,"id" desc
  • The direction must be asc or desc. Any other value throws an ArgumentError.
  • The column name is quoted, but a name with ( is kept as it is. Do not pass user input as the column name.

docs.title: limit, take and offset
docs.text:
limit and take do the same thing.

await Actor().limit(10).get();
await Actor().take(10).get();
await Actor().limit(10).offset(20).get();
// LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20

docs.title: groupBy
docs.text:
Takes one column, or a list of columns.

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await Actor()
    .select('count(*) as total, age')
    .groupBy('age')
    .get();

Info

A query with groupBy returns maps, not models. This is because a group row does not match a model row.

docs.title: Join
docs.text:
await Actor().join('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', 'actor.id').get();
// JOIN "actor_info" on "actor_info"."actor_id" = "actor"."id"

await Actor().leftJoin('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', 'actor.id').get();
await Actor().rightJoin('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', 'actor.id').get();

// with an operator
await Actor().join('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', '=', 'actor.id').get();

For a join condition that these methods can not build, use the raw methods. Nothing is quoted. Values go in the map, like in whereRaw.

await Actor().joinRaw('actor_info on actor_info.actor_id = actor.id').get();
await Actor().leftJoinRaw('actor_info on actor_info.actor_id = actor.id').get();
await Actor().rightJoinRaw(
  'actor_info on actor_info.actor_id = actor.id and actor_info.type = @type',
  <String, dynamic>{'type': 'main'},
).get();

Note

SQLite before 3.39 has no RIGHT JOIN.

docs.title: create and insert
docs.text:
create and insert do the same thing. They insert one row, then read it back and return it.

Actor actor = await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{
  'name': 'John Wick',
  'age': 60,
});
print(actor.id);
  • On a model, the result is the model. On QueryBuilder.table(...), the result is a map.
  • It works with any primary key type, for example a uuid string.
  • On a model with events, create calls save(), so the hooks run.

docs.title: insertMultiple
docs.text:
Inserts many rows in one query. It does not return models. On Postgres it returns the new ids, like [{id: 4}, {id: 5}]. On MySQL it returns only one id.

await Actor().insertMultiple(<Map<String, dynamic>>[
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick', 'age': 60},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Doe', 'age': 25},
]);

The columns are the keys from all rows. When a row does not have a key, that column gets its default value.

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
Updates all rows that match the where part.

await Actor()
    .where('id', 3)
    .where('status', 'active')
    .update(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Updated AJ', 'age': 120});
// UPDATE "actor" SET "name" = @name_p2,"age" = @age_p3
//   WHERE "id" = @id_p0 AND "status" = @status_p1

Warning

update without where changes every row of the table. A query update does not set updated_at and fires no model events. To do that, load the model, change it and call save().

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
Deletes all rows that match the where part.

await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').delete();
// DELETE FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = @name_p0

On a model with softDelete: true, delete sets deleted_at and keeps the row.

docs.title: forceDelete
docs.text:
On a model with softDelete: true, forceDelete really deletes the rows. It also deletes rows that are already soft deleted, so you do not need withTrash().

await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').forceDelete();

docs.title: withTrash
docs.text:
A model with softDelete: true hides soft deleted rows. withTrash() shows them too. On a model without soft deletes it does nothing.

List<Actor> actors = await Actor().withTrash().where('name', 'John Wick').get();

docs.title: truncate
docs.text:
Deletes all rows of the table and resets the id counter.

await Actor().truncate();
await Actor().truncate(resetId: false); // keep the id counter on Postgres and SQLite

On Postgres it runs TRUNCATE TABLE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE. On SQLite it runs DELETE FROM.

docs.title: toSql
docs.text:
Returns the SQL of the query with the values filled in. The values are not quoted or escaped, so use it only to read the query.

String sql = Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').toSql();
print(sql); // SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = John Wick

docs.title: debug
docs.text:
Prints the SQL and the values of the query when it runs.

await Actor().debug(true).where('age', 60).get();

To print all queries, set debug: true in the ConnectionConfig. See Database.

docs.title: Schema builder
docs.text:
The schema builder creates, changes and drops tables with Dart code. The same code works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. You mostly use it inside a migration.

await schema.create('posts', (Table table) {
  table.id();
  table.foreignId('user_id').constrained().cascadeOnDelete();
  table.string('title');
  table.text('body').nullable();
  table.enumeration('status', <String>['draft', 'published']).defaultTo('draft');
  table.timestamps();
});

docs.title: Get a schema
docs.text:
In a migration, up and down get a Schema. It runs on the migration connection.

Outside a migration, Schema() uses the query builder connection. You can also give a driver: Schema(driver).

Schema schema = Schema();
await schema.dropIfExists('posts');

docs.title: Tables
docs.text: Method What it does create('t', (Table table) {...}) Create table t. It fails when the table exists. table('t', (Table table) {...}) Change table t: add columns, change columns, keys. drop('t') Drop table t. It fails when the table is missing. dropIfExists('t') Drop table t when it exists. rename('from', 'to') Rename a table. hasTable('t') true when the table exists. hasColumn('t', 'c') true when the column exists. getColumnListing('t') The column names, in order.

docs.title: Column types
docs.text:
Method Postgres MySQL / MariaDB SQLite id() / bigIncrements('id') BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT increments('id') SERIAL PRIMARY KEY INT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT string('c', [255]) VARCHAR(n) VARCHAR(n) VARCHAR(n) char('c', [255]) CHAR(n) CHAR(n) CHAR(n) text('c') TEXT TEXT TEXT mediumText('c') TEXT MEDIUMTEXT TEXT longText('c') TEXT LONGTEXT TEXT integer('c') INTEGER INT INTEGER bigInteger('c') BIGINT BIGINT INTEGER smallInteger('c') SMALLINT SMALLINT INTEGER tinyInteger('c') SMALLINT TINYINT INTEGER unsignedInteger('c') (and unsignedBigInteger, unsignedSmallInteger, unsignedTinyInteger) signed type ... UNSIGNED INTEGER float('c') REAL FLOAT FLOAT double('c') DOUBLE PRECISION DOUBLE DOUBLE decimal('c', [8], [2]) DECIMAL(p, s) DECIMAL(p, s) DECIMAL(p, s) boolean('c') BOOLEAN TINYINT(1) BOOLEAN date('c') DATE DATE DATE dateTime('c') TIMESTAMP DATETIME DATETIME dateTimeTz('c') TIMESTAMPTZ DATETIME DATETIME time('c') TIME TIME TIME timestamp('c') TIMESTAMP TIMESTAMP TIMESTAMP timestampTz('c') TIMESTAMPTZ TIMESTAMP TIMESTAMP json('c') / jsonb('c') JSONB JSON JSON uuid(['uuid']) UUID CHAR(36) TEXT binary('c') BYTEA BLOB BLOB enumeration('c', ['a', 'b']) VARCHAR(255) + CHECK ENUM('a', 'b') VARCHAR(255) + CHECK foreignId('user_id') BIGINT BIGINT UNSIGNED INTEGER foreignUuid('user_id') UUID CHAR(36) TEXT

Helpers:

  • timestamps(): nullable created_at and updated_at (timestampTz).
  • softDeletes(['deleted_at']): nullable deleted_at (timestampTz), for models with softDelete: true.
  • rememberToken(): nullable remember_token VARCHAR(100).
  • morphs('owner'): owner_id (unsigned big integer), owner_type (string) and one index on both columns.

JSON on SQLite

SQLite has no JSON type. The column is declared as JSON, so the SQLite driver knows to decode it when you read it.

docs.title: Modifiers
docs.text:
Modifiers come after the column type. They can be chained: table.string('email').nullable().unique().

Modifier What it does Notes nullable() Allow NULL. Columns are NOT NULL by default. nullable(false) makes it NOT NULL again. defaultTo(value) Default value. Strings are escaped, so any text is safe. bool, numbers, null, Map/List (saved as JSON) and DateTime work too. withDefault is the old name. defaultRaw('sql') Default as raw SQL. It is not escaped. Put expressions in ( ): defaultRaw('(1 + 1)'). MySQL and SQLite need it. useCurrent() Default to the current time. Same as defaultRaw('CURRENT_TIMESTAMP'). useCurrentOnUpdate() Set the current time on each update. MySQL only. Postgres and SQLite ignore it. Set the time in your code there. unique() Add a unique index {table}_{column}_unique. index() Add an index {table}_{column}_index. primary() Make the column the primary key. unsigned() UNSIGNED. MySQL only. Others ignore it. comment('text') Column comment. Postgres and MySQL. SQLite ignores it. after('column') Put the new column after another one. MySQL only, only in schema.table. Others add it at the end. change() Change an existing column (in schema.table). See Change columns.

MySQL defaults on TEXT and JSON

MySQL only allows a default on TEXT, BLOB and JSON as an expression. The schema builder writes it as DEFAULT ('value') for you.

docs.title: Change a table
docs.text:
await schema.table('users', (Table table) {
  table.string('avatar').nullable().after('email'); // add
  table.string('name', 100).nullable().change();    // change
  table.renameColumn('bio', 'about');
  table.dropColumn('age');
  table.dropColumns(<String>['a', 'b']);
});

A column in schema.table is added. Add .change() to change a column that exists.

docs.title: Change columns
docs.text:
change() sets the full new column: type, null, default and comment. Give every modifier you want to keep.

// before: string('title') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'x'
table.string('title', 500).nullable().defaultTo('x').change();

How it runs:

Driver SQL Postgres One ALTER TABLE: ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE ... USING col::type, SET/DROP NOT NULL, SET/DROP DEFAULT, and the enum CHECK again. MySQL ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN <full column>. SQLite SQLite can not change a column. Dox makes the table again (see below).

change() with unique() or index() adds the index. It fails when the index already exists.

docs.title: Indexes and keys
docs.text:
columns is a column name or a list of names.

table.index(<String>['state', 'created_at']);  // posts_state_created_at_index
table.unique('slug');                          // posts_slug_unique
table.primary(<String>['post_id', 'tag_id']);  // composite primary key

table.dropIndex(<String>['state', 'created_at']); // by columns
table.dropUnique('posts_slug_unique');            // or by name

Index names are {table}_{columns}_{index|unique|foreign}. You can give your own name as the last argument: table.unique('slug', 'my_name').

docs.title: Foreign keys
docs.text:
table.foreignId('user_id').constrained().cascadeOnDelete();
// same as:
table.foreignId('user_id');
table.foreign('user_id').references('id').on('users').onDelete('cascade');
  • constrained([table], [column = 'id']) guesses the table from the column: user_id becomes users, category_id becomes categories. Dox models use singular table names by default (User is user). If your table is singular, give it: constrained('user').
  • Actions: onDelete('cascade' | 'set null' | 'restrict' | 'no action'), onUpdate(...), and the short ones cascadeOnDelete(), nullOnDelete(), restrictOnDelete(), cascadeOnUpdate().
  • Put nullable() before constrained(): table.foreignId('editor_id').nullable().constrained('users').
  • Drop it: table.dropForeign(<String>['user_id']) or table.dropForeign('posts_user_id_foreign').

Same type on both sides

id() is a big integer. foreignId() is a big integer too, so they match. If the parent uses increments() (a normal integer), use unsignedInteger() for the child on MySQL.

docs.title: SQLite notes
docs.text:
SQLite ALTER TABLE can only add, rename and drop columns. For these changes, Dox makes the table again:

  • change() of a column,
  • foreign(...) on an existing table,
  • dropForeign(...).

It makes a new table with the change, copies the rows, drops the old table and renames the new one. It keeps the columns, primary key, AUTOINCREMENT, foreign keys, indexes and enum checks. All of it runs in one transaction. It fails on tables with other CHECK constraints or with generated columns.

Other SQLite limits:

  • primary(...) on an existing table is not supported.
  • A new column that is NOT NULL needs a default. A new column can not default to CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.
  • dropColumn fails when the column is in an index or a foreign key. Drop those first.

docs.title: Per driver notes
docs.text: Feature Postgres MySQL / MariaDB SQLite enumeration CHECK (col IN (...)) ENUM(...) CHECK (col IN (...)) unsigned ignored UNSIGNED ignored comment COMMENT ON COLUMN inline COMMENT ignored after ignored AFTER col ignored useCurrentOnUpdate ignored ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ignored change() ALTER COLUMN MODIFY COLUMN table rebuild add/drop foreign key on a table ALTER TABLE ALTER TABLE table rebuild schema changes in a transaction yes no, saved right away yes index name length 63 64 no limit

docs.title: See the SQL
docs.text:
Every change is a Table blueprint. A grammar turns it into SQL, without a database:

Table table = Table('users', creating: true)
  ..id()
  ..string('email').unique();
print(table.toSql(PostgresGrammar()));
// [CREATE TABLE "users" ("id" BIGSERIAL NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, "email" VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL),
//  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "users_email_unique" ON "users" ("email")]

Grammars: PostgresGrammar, MysqlGrammar and SqliteGrammar. On SQLite, the changes that need a table rebuild only run on a database.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A transaction runs many queries as one unit. Either all of them are saved, or none of them.

QueryBuilder.transaction() takes a function:

  • It commits when the function ends.
  • It rolls back when the function throws. Then the error is thrown again.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
// a transaction
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Actor actor = Actor();
  actor.name = 'John Wick';
  await actor.save();
  await QueryBuilder.table('actor_info').insert(<String, dynamic>{
    'actor_id': actor.id,
  });
});

// return a value
int? id = await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Actor actor = Actor();
  actor.name = 'John Wick';
  await actor.save();
  return actor.id;
});

// on another connection
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  // ...
}, connection: 'mysql');
  • All queries and models inside the function use the transaction. You do not pass a transaction object around.
  • A transaction inside another transaction joins the outer one. There are no savepoints. If the inner one throws, the whole outer transaction rolls back.

MySQL

On MySQL and MariaDB, CREATE, ALTER and DROP TABLE are saved right away. A rollback can not undo them.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
• Postgres and MySQL use a connection pool. Set the size with maxConnectionCount in the extra map of the connection.
