  • A transaction uses one connection of the pool. Other queries use the other connections.
  • SQLite has one connection per isolate. While a transaction is open, the other queries of that isolate wait.
  • Values are always sent as bound parameters. They are never written into the SQL text.

Changed in 3.x

Before 3.x, Postgres ran every query in its own transaction. Now a query only runs in a transaction when you use QueryBuilder.transaction().

docs.title: Model
docs.text: A model is a Dart class for one database table. You read, create, change and delete rows through the model. A model has all the query builder methods too.

docs.title: Create a model
docs.text:
dox create:model Blog      # only the model
dox create:model Blog -m   # the model and a migration for the table `blogs`

This makes lib/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart. make:model is another name for the same command.

The model code uses a generated class (BlogGenerator). Run the generator after you make or change a model:

dart run build_runner build

dart run build_runner watch runs the generator again each time you save a file.

docs.title: A model
Model options
docs.text:
All options go in @DoxModel(...).

Option Default What it does table class name in snake_case The table name. primaryKey 'id' The primary key column. createdAt 'created_at' The column that keeps the create time. updatedAt 'updated_at' The column that keeps the last update time. softDelete false delete() sets deleted_at and keeps the row.

docs.title: table
docs.text:
The default table name is the class name in snake_case, and singular. Blog uses blog, and BlogPost uses blog_post.

@DoxModel(table: 'blogs')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

Info

dox create:model Blog -m sets table: 'blogs' for you, because the migration makes the plural table blogs.

docs.title: primaryKey
docs.text:
@DoxModel(primaryKey: 'uid')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

The field name is the key in camelCase. With primaryKey: 'blog_id', the field is blogId.

docs.title: createdAt and updatedAt
docs.text:
save() sets these columns to the current UTC time. Use the options when your columns have other names.

@DoxModel(createdAt: 'created', updatedAt: 'modified')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

Read the values with blog.createdAt and blog.updatedAt.

docs.title: softDelete
docs.text:
@DoxModel(softDelete: true)
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

The table needs a nullable deleted_at column. In a migration, add table.softDeletes();.

  • delete() sets deleted_at to the current time. The row stays in the table.
  • Queries do not return soft deleted rows. Use withTrash() to get them too.
  • forceDelete() really deletes the row.
  • restore() sets deleted_at back to NULL.

docs.title: Column name
docs.text:
The default column name is the field name in snake_case. Use name when the column has another name.

@Column()
String? userId; // column: user_id

@Column(name: 'body')
String? description; // column: body

docs.title: Field types
docs.text:
The field type tells Dox how to read the value.

Field type Column String? text, varchar int? integer types double? float, double. MySQL also gives DECIMAL as double. Postgres gives numeric as String. bool? boolean DateTime? date, datetime, timestamp Map<String, dynamic>? or List<dynamic>? JSON

For other conversions, use beforeSave and beforeGet.

docs.title: beforeSave and beforeGet
docs.text:
These options take a static function of the model class. The function gets a map and returns the value.

  • beforeSave runs before a save. It gets the model values (column name => value). It returns the value to save in this column.
  • beforeGet runs when a row is read. It gets the row from the database. It returns the value for this field.
@DoxModel()
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  // beforeSave: make the slug from the title
  @Column(beforeSave: makeSlug)
  String? slug;

  // beforeGet: old rows have no status, show them as draft
  @Column(beforeGet: readStatus)
  String? status;

  static String? makeSlug(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
    return map['title']?.toString().toLowerCase().replaceAll(' ', '-');
  }

  static String? readStatus(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
    return map['status'] as String? ?? 'draft';
  }
}

docs.title: Save
docs.text:
save() inserts a new model, or updates a model that has an id.

// insert
Blog blog = Blog();
blog.title = 'My first blog';
await blog.save();
print(blog.id); // the new id

// update
Blog? found = await Blog().find(1);
found?.title = 'New title';
await found?.save();

// set a field to null
found?.slug = null;
await found?.save(); // slug is now NULL in the database

// create from a map
Blog created = await Blog().create(<String, dynamic>{
  'title': 'My first blog',
  'status': 'draft',
});
  • On insert, null fields are not sent, so the database default is used.
  • On update, a field is set to NULL only when it had a value before (loaded from the database, or saved). Fields that were not loaded, for example with select(), are not changed.
  • save() returns false when a model event cancels it.

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
// delete a record
Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
await blog?.delete(); // deletes only this record

// force delete
Blog? trashed = await Blog().withTrash().find(1);
await trashed?.forceDelete(); // deletes the row, also with softDelete

// restore
Blog? deleted = await Blog().withTrash().find(1);
await deleted?.restore(); // sets deleted_at back to NULL

save(), delete(), forceDelete() and restore() fire model events.

docs.title: Convert to a map or JSON
docs.text:
Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);

Map<String, dynamic>? map = blog?.toMap();  // all columns and computed values
Map<String, dynamic>? json = blog?.toJson(); // the same, without hidden fields
Map<String, dynamic>? row = blog?.toMap(original: true); // the raw database row

jsonEncode(blog) uses toJson(). So you can return a model, or a list of models, from a controller.

docs.title: Hide fields
docs.text:
Fields in hidden are left out of toJson(). Use the column names.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password', 'remember_token'];
}

docs.title: Computed values
docs.text:
A computed value is a getter that is added to toJson() and toMap(). It is like $appends with an accessor in Laravel.

Add @Computed() to a getter in the model, then run dart run build_runner build.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column(name: 'first_name')
  String? firstName;

  @Column(name: 'last_name')
  String? lastName;

  @Computed() // json key: full_name
  String get fullName => '$firstName $lastName';

  @Computed(name: 'initials') // custom json key
  String get shortName => '${firstName?[0]}${lastName?[0]}';
}

User? user = await User().find(1);
print(user?.toJson());
// {id: 1, first_name: John, last_name: Wick, ..., full_name: John Wick, initials: JW}
  • The default key is the getter name in snake_case (fullName becomes full_name).
  • A computed value is never a column. It is not read from the database, and it is not sent in INSERT or UPDATE.
  • hidden also hides computed values. Use the json key, for example ['full_name'].
  • Computed values of loaded relations are in the nested JSON too.
  • toMap(original: true) returns the raw database row, so it has no computed values.
  • A getter runs each time toJson() or toMap() is called, so keep it fast.

No reflection

build_runner makes the code. There is no reflection at run time. A model without @Computed() does no extra work in toJson().

docs.title: New query
docs.text:
A model object keeps the parts of its query (where, orderBy, ...). query() gives a new, empty model, so you can start another query.

Blog blog = Blog();
List<Blog> active = await blog.where('status', 'active').get();

// a new query, without the where above
List<Blog> deleted = await blog.query().where('status', 'deleted').get();

docs.title: Debug
docs.text:
debug(true) prints the SQL of this model in the terminal.

Blog blog = Blog();
blog.debug(true);
blog.title = 'John Wick';
await blog.save();

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
A model can load related models. See HasOne, HasMany, BelongsTo and ManyToMany.

The relationship pages use these tables:

erDiagram
    user ||--o| user_info : "HasOne"
    user ||--o{ post : "HasMany"
    user ||--o{ comment : "BelongsTo, from comment"
    artist ||--o{ artist_song : "ManyToMany"
    song ||--o{ artist_song : "ManyToMany"
    user {
        int id PK
        string name
    }
    user_info {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string address
    }
    post {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string title
    }
    comment {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string content
    }
    artist_song {
        int id PK
        int artist_id FK
        int song_id FK
    }

docs.title: Model events
docs.text: A model fires events when you save, delete or restore it. You can run your own code on these events. There are two ways: hooks in the model, and observer classes.

docs.title: Hooks in the model
docs.text:
Override an on... method in the model. Then run dart run build_runner build.

@DoxModel(softDelete: true)
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? email;

  @override
  Future<void> onCreating() async {
    email = email?.trim().toLowerCase();
  }

  @override
  Future<void> onDeleted() async {
    await AuditLog().create({'message': 'user $id deleted'});
  }
}

Info

The hook names start with on (onCreating, not creating). This is because created and deleted are common column names. Declare the hooks in the model class itself. The generator looks there.

docs.title: Events and order
docs.text:
Call Events, in order save() on a new model saving → creating → INSERT → created → saved save() on a loaded model saving → updating → UPDATE → updated → saved create({...}) the same as save() on a new model delete() deleting → DELETE or soft delete → deleted forceDelete() forceDeleting → deleting → DELETE → deleted → forceDeleted restore() restoring → UPDATE deleted_at = NULL → restored

The model hook runs first. Then the observers run, in the order you added them.

Query updates and deletes fire no events

Events fire only on a model instance. User().where('active', false).update({...}), User().where(...).delete() and insertMultiple() run one query and fire no events. This is the same as Laravel.

docs.title: Cancel an operation
docs.text:
Throw CancelModelEvent in a "before" event (saving, creating, updating, deleting, forceDeleting, restoring). The query does not run. save(), delete(), forceDelete() and restore() return false.

@override
Future<void> onDeleting() async {
  if (isAdmin == true) throw CancelModelEvent('admins can not be deleted');
}

bool deleted = await user.delete(); // false

create({...}) returns the unsaved model (its id is null) when an event cancels it. Any other error from a hook is thrown to the caller.

docs.title: Observers
docs.text:
An observer is a class that listens to one model. Override only the methods you need. Each method gets the model.

class UserObserver extends ModelObserver<User> {
  final Mailer mailer;

  UserObserver(this.mailer);

  @override
  Future<void> created(User user) async {
    await mailer.sendWelcome(user.email!);
  }
}

Add it once, for example when the app starts:

Model.observe<User>(UserObserver(mailer));
  • You can add more than one observer to a model.
  • Model.forgetObservers<User>() removes the observers of User. Model.forgetObservers() removes all.

docs.title: Skip events
docs.text:
await user.saveQuietly(); // save without events

await Model.withoutEvents(() async {
  await user.save();
  await post.delete();
});

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
Hooks run inside the transaction of the caller. save() does not start a transaction by itself.

  • If an "after" hook (created, saved, ...) throws, the row is already written.
  • To undo the row when a hook fails, wrap the call in QueryBuilder.transaction():
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await user.save(); // if onCreated() throws, the INSERT is rolled back
});

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• There is no reflection. The generator sets hasModelHooks only for models that declare a hook.
  • A model with no hooks and no observers does no event work. It is one bool check, plus one map lookup when some other model has observers.
  • When a model has events, create({...}) fills a model with fromMap() and calls save(). Only the @Column fields are saved then.

docs.title: Serializer
docs.text:
A serializer changes how a model looks in the HTTP response. Use it when the JSON keys or values must be different from the model columns.

Tip

You do not always need a serializer. A model can be returned from a controller as it is. Dox sends toJson(). To only hide fields, use hidden.

docs.title: Create a serializer
docs.text:
dox create:serializer Blog

This makes lib/app/http/serializers/blog.serializer.dart.

docs.title: Use
BelongsTo
docs.text:
Use BelongsTo when this table keeps the foreign key to another table. For example, a comment belongs to a user. The comment table has the column user_id.

BelongsTo is the other side of HasOne and HasMany.

docs.title: Define it
docs.text:
Add a field with @BelongsTo(...) to the model. The field type is the related model, nullable.

lib/app/models/comment/comment.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../user/user.model.dart';

part 'comment.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Comment extends CommentGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? content;

  @BelongsTo(User)
  User? user;
}
lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? status;
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Load it
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Load it in one of these ways. Use the field name ('user') as the relation name.

docs.title: preload
docs.text:
Use it when you load the models with a query.

List<Comment> comments = await Comment().preload('user').all();
for (Comment comment in comments) {
  print(comment.user?.name);
}

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst. It runs one query for all comments, not one query per comment.

docs.title: $getRelation
docs.text:
Use it when you already have the model.

Comment? comment = await Comment().find(1);
await comment?.$getRelation('user');
print(comment?.user?.name);

Do not call it in a loop over many models. Use preload for a list.

docs.title: related
docs.text:
Use it when you need more conditions on the related row.

Comment? comment = await Comment().find(1);
User? activeUser = await comment
    ?.related<User>('user')
    ?.where('status', 'active')
    .getFirst();

related gives a query. You can add more conditions before you run it. It does not set comment.user.

docs.title: eager
docs.text:
Use it when every query of Comment should load the relation.

@BelongsTo(User, eager: true)
User? user;

With eager: true, every query of Comment loads the relation. You do not call preload.

The load runs this SQL:

SELECT "user".*, "comment"."id" as "_foreign_id" FROM "user"
  LEFT JOIN "comment" on "comment"."user_id" = "user"."id"
  WHERE "comment"."user_id" IN (@commentuser_id_p0, ...)

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default What it is foreignKey {related table}_id, like user_id The column in this table that points to the related model. localKey the primary key of the related model The column in the related table that foreignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

Custom table names

The default foreignKey uses the table name of the related model, not its class name. When User has @DoxModel(table: 'users'), the default is users_id. Then set foreignKey: 'user_id' yourself.

docs.title: foreignKey and localKey
docs.text:
@BelongsTo(User, foreignKey: 'author_id', localKey: 'id')
User? author;

docs.title: onQuery
docs.text:
onQuery is a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it.

@DoxModel()
class Comment extends CommentGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId;

  @BelongsTo(User, onQuery: onlyActive)
  User? activeUser;

  static QueryBuilder<User> onlyActive(User q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active');
  }
}

docs.title: In JSON
docs.text:
• A relation with eager: true is always in toJson().
  • A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query.
  • The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: user.

Known issue: names with more than one word

For a relation without eager: true, toJson() looks for the snake_case name in the preload list. But preload needs the field name ('activeUser'). So a preloaded activeUser is on the model, but it is not in toJson(). Use a one word field name, or eager: true, when you need it in JSON.

docs.title: HasMany
docs.text: Use HasMany when one row of this table has many rows in another table. For example, a user has many posts. The other table keeps the foreign key (post.user_id).

docs.title: Define it
docs.text:
Add a field with @HasMany(...) to the model. The field type is a list of the related model. Start it as an empty list.

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../post/post.model.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];
}
lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'post.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? status;
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Load it
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Load it in one of these ways. Use the field name ('posts') as the relation name.

docs.title: preload
docs.text:
Use it when you load the models with a query.

User? user = await User().preload('posts').find(1);
print(user?.posts.length);

List<User> users = await User().preload('posts').get();

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst. For a list of users, it runs one query for all of them. A user without posts gets an empty list.

docs.title: $getRelation
docs.text:
Use it when you already have the model.

User? user = await User().find(1);
await user?.$getRelation('posts');
print(user?.posts.length);

docs.title: related
docs.text:
Use it when you need more conditions on the related rows.

User? user = await User().find(1);
List<Post> activePosts = await user
        ?.related<Post>('posts')
        ?.where('status', 'active')
        .orderBy('id', 'desc')
        .get() ??
    <Post>[];

related gives a query. You can add more conditions before you run it. It does not set user.posts.

docs.title: eager
docs.text:
Use it when every query of User should load the relation.

@HasMany(Post, eager: true)
List<Post> posts = <Post>[];

With eager: true, every query of User loads the relation. You do not call preload.

The load runs this SQL:

SELECT *, "user_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "post" WHERE "user_id" IN (@user_id_p0, ...)

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default What it is foreignKey {this table}_id, like user_id The column in the related table that points to this model. localKey the primary key of this model The column in this table that foreignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

Custom table names

The default foreignKey uses the table name, not the class name. With @DoxModel(table: 'users'), the default is users_id. Then set foreignKey: 'user_id' yourself.

docs.title: foreignKey and localKey
docs.text:
@HasMany(Book, foreignKey: 'author_code', localKey: 'code')
List<Book> books = <Book>[];

docs.title: onQuery
docs.text:
onQuery is a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it. You can have two fields on the same model with different queries.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];

  @HasMany(Post, onQuery: onlyActive)
  List<Post> activePosts = <Post>[];

  static QueryBuilder<Post> onlyActive(Post q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active').orderBy('id', 'desc');
  }
}

docs.title: In JSON
docs.text:
• A relation with eager: true is always in toJson().
  • A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query.
  • The JSON key is the field name in snake_case.

Known issue: names with more than one word

For a relation without eager: true, toJson() looks for the snake_case name in the preload list. But preload needs the field name ('activePosts'). So a preloaded activePosts is on the model, but it is not in toJson(). Use a one word field name, or eager: true, when you need it in JSON.

docs.title: HasOne
docs.text: Use HasOne when one row of this table has one row in another table. For example, a user has one user info row. The other table keeps the foreign key (user_info.user_id).

docs.title: Define it
docs.text:
Add a field with @HasOne(...) to the model. The field type is the related model, nullable.

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../user_info/user_info.model.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @HasOne(UserInfo)
  UserInfo? userInfo;
}
lib/app/models/user_info/user_info.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user_info.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class UserInfo extends UserInfoGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? address;
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Load it
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Load it in one of these ways. Use the field name ('userInfo') as the relation name.

docs.title: preload
docs.text:
Use it when you load the models with a query.

User? user = await User().preload('userInfo').find(1);
print(user?.userInfo?.address);

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst. For a list of users, it runs one query for all of them.

docs.title: $getRelation
docs.text:
Use it when you already have the model.

User? user = await User().find(1);
await user?.$getRelation('userInfo');
print(user?.userInfo?.address);

docs.title: related
docs.text:
Use it when you need more conditions on the related row.

User? user = await User().find(1);
UserInfo? info = await user
    ?.related<UserInfo>('userInfo')
    ?.where('address', '!=', '')
    .getFirst();

related gives a query. You can add more conditions before you run it. It does not set user.userInfo.

docs.title: eager
docs.text:
Use it when every query of User should load the relation.

@HasOne(UserInfo, eager: true)
UserInfo? userInfo;

With eager: true, every query of User loads the relation. You do not call preload.

The load runs this SQL:

SELECT *, "user_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "user_info" WHERE "user_id" IN (@user_id_p0)

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default What it is foreignKey {this table}_id, like user_id The column in the related table that points to this model. localKey the primary key of this model The column in this table that foreignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

Custom table names

The default foreignKey uses the table name, not the class name. With @DoxModel(table: 'users'), the default is users_id. Then set foreignKey: 'user_id' yourself.

docs.title: foreignKey and localKey
docs.text:
@HasOne(UserInfo, foreignKey: 'owner_id', localKey: 'id')
UserInfo? userInfo;

docs.title: onQuery
docs.text:
onQuery is a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasOne(UserInfo, onQuery: onlyActive)
  UserInfo? userInfo;

  static QueryBuilder<UserInfo> onlyActive(UserInfo q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active');
  }
}

docs.title: In JSON
docs.text:
• A relation with eager: true is always in toJson().
  • A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query.
  • The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: user_info.

Known issue: names with more than one word

For a relation without eager: true, toJson() looks for the snake_case name in the preload list. But preload needs the field name ('userInfo'). So a preloaded userInfo is on the model, but it is not in toJson(). Use a one word field name (like info), or eager: true, when you need it in JSON.

docs.title: ManyToMany
docs.text:
Use ManyToMany when rows on both sides can have many rows on the other side. For example, an artist has many songs, and a song has many artists.

The link is kept in a third table, the pivot table. It has one foreign key to each side.

docs.title: Tables
Define it
docs.text:
Add a field with @ManyToMany(...) to each model that needs it. The field type is a list of the related model. Start it as an empty list.

lib/app/models/artist/artist.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../song/song.model.dart';

part 'artist.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Artist extends ArtistGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @ManyToMany(Song)
  List<Song> songs = <Song>[];
}
lib/app/models/song/song.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../artist/artist.model.dart';

part 'song.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Song extends SongGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @ManyToMany(Artist)
  List<Artist> artists = <Artist>[];
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Load it
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Load it in one of these ways. Use the field name ('songs') as the relation name.

docs.title: preload
docs.text:
Use it when you load the models with a query.

Artist? artist = await Artist().preload('songs').find(1);
print(artist?.songs.length);

List<Song> songs = await Song().preload('artists').get();

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst. For a list of models, it runs one query for all of them. A model without links gets an empty list.

docs.title: $getRelation
docs.text:
Use it when you already have the model.

Artist? artist = await Artist().find(1);
await artist?.$getRelation('songs');
print(artist?.songs.length);

docs.title: related
docs.text:
Use it when you need more conditions on the related rows.

Artist? artist = await Artist().find(1);
List<Song> songs = await artist
        ?.related<Song>('songs')
        ?.orderBy('song.title')
        .get() ??
    <Song>[];

related gives a query. You can add more conditions before you run it. It does not set artist.songs. The query joins the pivot table, so write table.column for column names.

docs.title: eager
docs.text:
Use it when every query of Artist should load the relation.

@ManyToMany(Song, eager: true)
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];

With eager: true, every query of Artist loads the relation. You do not call preload. Do not set eager: true on both sides. Each side would load the other side again and again.

The load runs this SQL:

SELECT "song".*, "artist_song"."artist_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "song"
  LEFT JOIN "artist_song" on "artist_song"."song_id" = "song"."id"
  WHERE "artist_song"."artist_id" IN (@artist_songartist_id_p0, ...)

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The examples are for @ManyToMany(Song) in the Artist model.

Option Default Example value What it is pivotTable the two table names in A-Z order, joined with _ artist_song The pivot table. pivotForeignKey {this table}_id artist_id The pivot column that points to this model. pivotRelatedForeignKey {related table}_id song_id The pivot column that points to the related model. localKey the primary key of this model id The column in artist that pivotForeignKey points to. relatedKey the primary key of the related model id The column in song that pivotRelatedForeignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

Default pivot table names:

  • artist and song give artist_song.
  • blog and category give blog_category.

Custom table names

The defaults use the table names, not the class names. With @DoxModel(table: 'artists'), the default pivot table is artists_song and the default pivotForeignKey is artists_id. Then set the options yourself.

docs.title: Set all keys
docs.text:
@ManyToMany(
  Song,
  pivotTable: 'artist_song',
  pivotForeignKey: 'artist_id',
  pivotRelatedForeignKey: 'song_id',
  localKey: 'id',
  relatedKey: 'id',
)
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];

docs.title: onQuery
docs.text:
onQuery is a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it.

@DoxModel()
class Artist extends ArtistGenerator {
  @ManyToMany(Song, onQuery: onlyPublished)
  List<Song> songs = <Song>[];

  static QueryBuilder<Song> onlyPublished(Song q) {
    return q.where('song.status', 'published');
  }
}

docs.title: In JSON
docs.text:
• A relation with eager: true is always in toJson().
  • A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query.
  • The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: songs.

Known issue: names with more than one word

For a relation without eager: true, toJson() looks for the snake_case name in the preload list. But preload needs the field name, like 'topSongs'. So a preloaded topSongs is on the model, but it is not in toJson(). Use a one word field name, or eager: true, when you need it in JSON.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text: Cache() keeps data that is slow to make, so the next request can read it fast. It runs on dox_cache, which is built into dox_core.

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text:
Driver Where the data is Shared between isolates Locks file files in a folder (default storage/cache) yes, on the same machine no memory a map inside the isolate no yes redis a Redis server yes, also between machines yes null nowhere. It stores nothing - no

Many isolates

Dox runs one isolate per CPU core. Each isolate has its own memory store. So a value you put in one isolate is missing in the others. Use redis when all isolates and servers must see the same data.

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
Without a config, Dox has a file store (the default) and a memory store. To change the stores, make lib/config/cache.dart:

lib/config/cache.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

CacheConfig cache = CacheConfig(
  defaultStore: env.cacheStore,
  stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'file': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'file', 'path': 'storage/cache'},
    'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory', 'max_size': 10000},
    'redis': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'redis',
      'host': env.redisHost,
      'port': env.redisPort,
      'prefix': 'app_cache:',
    },
  },
);

Redis needs two keys that a new project does not have yet. Add them to lib/config/env.dart and run dart run build_runner build:

lib/config/env.dart
  String get redisHost => '127.0.0.1';

  int get redisPort => 6379;

Then pass it to AppConfig(cache: cache) in lib/config/app.dart. Each store is made once per isolate, the first time you use it.

docs.title: Store options
docs.text:
Driver Options file path (default storage/cache), prefix memory max_size: the most items. When it is full, the item that was used least recently is removed. No limit by default. Also prefix. redis host (default 127.0.0.1), port (default 6379), username, password, db (default 0), tls (true/false), pool_size, prefix

The default prefix is dox_cache:.

docs.title: Redis pool_size
docs.text:
pool_size is the most Redis connections that one store opens in one isolate. The default is 10.

You rarely need to change it. A store sends all commands on one connection. It opens more connections only while a blocking command (like BLPOP) waits, and the cache does not send blocking commands. So each isolate uses about one connection: 4 isolates use about 4 connections.

docs.title: Values are JSON
docs.text: A value must be a JSON type: Map, List, String, num, bool or null. A Map comes back as Map<String, dynamic>. A List comes back as List<dynamic>.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
// no duration: the value stays forever
await Cache().put('foo', 'bar');
await Cache().put('foo', 'bar', duration: Duration(minutes: 10));

await Cache().get('foo');             // 'bar', or null when missing
await Cache().get('foo', 'default');  // 'default' when missing
await Cache().has('foo');             // true
await Cache().forget('foo');          // remove one key
await Cache().forever('settings', <String, dynamic>{'theme': 'dark'});
await Cache().flush();                // remove all items of the store

docs.title: remember
docs.text:
remember reads the value from the cache. When it is missing, the function runs and its result is stored.

List<dynamic> posts = await Cache().remember(
  'posts',
  Duration(minutes: 5),
  () => Post().all(),
);

rememberForever(key, fn) does the same with no expiry.

docs.title: getRaw
docs.text:
get decodes the stored JSON text into Dart values. If you then send the value as a JSON response, Dox must encode it again. That is double work.

getRaw gives the stored JSON text as it is. You can send it with no decode and no encode:

String? json = await Cache().getRaw('posts');
if (json != null) {
  return response(json).contentType(ContentType.json);
}

A missing key gives null. A stored String comes back as JSON, with its quotes: "bar".

docs.title: Another store
docs.text:
store(name) uses a store from the config instead of the default store:

await Cache().store('redis').put('foo', 'bar');
await Cache().store('memory').get('foo');

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Put items under a tag. Then you can remove only the items of that tag:

await Cache().tag('users').put('u1', 'Ann');
await Cache().tag('users').flush(); // removes only the items of this tag

tags(['a', 'b']) uses many tags.

docs.title: Locks
docs.text:
A lock makes sure only one request (or one server) runs some code at a time. The memory and redis stores support locks. Use redis when many isolates must share the lock.

CacheLock lock = Cache().store('redis').lock('report', Duration(seconds: 30));
if (await lock.get()) {
  try {
    await buildReport();
  } finally {
    await lock.release();
  }
}
  • get() tries once. It is true when you got the lock.
  • block(Duration(seconds: 5)) tries again and again until the time is over.
  • The lock is freed after its ttl, even if you never call release().

docs.title: More methods
docs.text:
Method What it does add(key, value, duration:) store only when the key is missing. true when it was stored pull(key) get the value and remove it increment(key, [by]) / decrement(key, [by]) change an integer. A missing key starts at 0 repository the dox_cache CacheStore, for everything else

See dox_cache for custom drivers.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Dox().cache is the CacheManager that Cache() uses. Replace it in a test, so the test needs no files and no Redis:

Dox().cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(
  defaultStore: 'memory',
  stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
  },
));

See Testing.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
This page shows how to build a Dox app for production and run it safely.

Never run production with dart run

dart run (and dox serve) uses the JIT compiler. It is made for development. It uses about 25x more memory at start (around 390 MB instead of 16 MB) and starts slower. Always build an AOT binary for production.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Compile the app to a native binary (AOT).

dox build

This makes a build/bundle/ folder:

File What it is build/bundle/bin/server the native binary. No Dart SDK needed to run it build/bundle/lib/ native libraries from build hooks (eg. SQLite) build/bundle/db/ your migrations build/bundle/.env.example copy it to build/bundle/.env, or use env variables

dox build runs build_runner first (when your app uses it). Then it runs dart build cli --target bin/server.dart --output build. It exits with code 1 when a step fails, so CI can stop.

Not dart compile exe

dox_orm depends on sqlite3 v3. It bundles SQLite with a build hook. dart compile exe does not run build hooks, so it stops with an error. dart build cli is the same AOT compiler and runs the hooks. Keep bin/ and lib/ together: the binary loads the libraries from ../lib.

Start the application.

cd build/bundle
./bin/server

The binary reads .env and db/ from the folder you start it in. A real environment variable wins over the .env file.

A new Dox app runs the migrations in bin/server.dart, before the server starts. So the database is up to date when the first request comes in.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
The Dockerfile in a new Dox app is a multi-stage build:

  1. The dart:stable image builds the AOT bundle with dart build cli --target bin/server.dart --output build.
  2. The final image is FROM scratch. It holds only the Dart AOT runtime files (/runtime/ from the dart image), the bundle (/app/bin/server and /app/lib/), db/ and an empty /tmp.
FROM dart:stable AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get
COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline
RUN dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
RUN dart build cli --target bin/server.dart --output build
RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ \
  && cp -r db /out/app/db

FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]

The image has no .env file, so secrets stay out of it. Pass config as environment variables.

docker build -t my-app .
docker run -p 3000:3000 -e APP_PORT=3000 -e APP_KEY=... -e DB_HOST=... my-app

Or use env_file: .env in docker-compose.yml.

docs.title: HTTPS: put a proxy in front
docs.text:
Do not serve HTTPS from Dart. TLS in Dart's HttpServer is slow (a known Dart SDK issue). Dox has no bindSecure.

Run Dox on plain HTTP on a private port. Put Caddy or nginx in front of it. The proxy does TLS, HTTP/2 and gzip.

The whole setup looks like this:

flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|HTTPS| X["Caddy or nginx<br>TLS, HTTP/2, gzip, body size limit"]
    X -->|"plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1:3000"| D["Dox binary<br>bin/server, one isolate per core"]
    D -->|"one pool per isolate"| DB[("Database")]
    M["Migrations<br>bin/server.dart runs them once, before the server starts"] --> DB

Then tell Dox to trust the proxy, so req.ip() and req.scheme() show the real client:

AppConfig(
  /// the proxy's IP, or a range like '10.0.0.0/8', or '172.16.0.0/12' for docker
  trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1'],
);
  • req.ip() reads X-Forwarded-For. Dox walks the list from the right and skips your proxies, so a fake value from the client is ignored.
  • req.scheme() reads X-Forwarded-Proto (http or https). req.isSecure() is true for https.
  • trustedProxies is empty by default. Then Dox ignores those headers, because any client can send them.
  • ['*'] trusts everyone. Only use it when the app port is not reachable from outside.

docs.title: Caddy
docs.text:
Caddy gets a certificate for you and sets X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto. Websockets work with no extra config.

example.com {
  encode gzip
  reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000
}

docs.title: Nginx
docs.text:
upstream dox {
  server 127.0.0.1:3000;
  keepalive 64;
}

map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
  default upgrade;
  ''      '';
}

server {
  listen 443 ssl http2;
  server_name example.com;

  ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem;
  ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem;

  # match maxMultipartSize in AppConfig
  client_max_body_size 100m;

  gzip on;
  gzip_types application/json text/plain text/css application/javascript;

  location / {
    proxy_pass http://dox;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;

    # websocket upgrade
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;

    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

    # stream uploads to Dox, do not buffer them in nginx first
    proxy_request_buffering off;
  }
}

server {
  listen 80;
  server_name example.com;
  return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}

docs.title: Keep it running
docs.text:
Dox uses all CPU cores by default (see Isolate).

  • When a worker isolate dies, Dox prints the error and starts it again.
  • When the main isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. Let a supervisor restart it: restart: unless-stopped in Docker compose, or Restart=always in systemd.
# /etc/systemd/system/dox.service
[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/srv/app/build/bundle
ExecStart=/srv/app/build/bundle/bin/server
EnvironmentFile=/srv/app/build/bundle/.env
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

docs.title: Many processes or machines
docs.text:
One Dox process already uses every core. You only need more processes to run on more machines, or to restart one process without downtime. Run each one on its own port (or machine) and list them in the proxy:

upstream dox {
  server 10.0.0.11:3000;
  server 10.0.0.12:3000;
  keepalive 64;
}

Websocket rooms then need a shared adapter (like Redis), because each process has its own memory.

docs.title: Dox CLI
docs.text:
The dox CLI creates projects and files, runs the dev server, builds for production and runs migrations.

Run dox help to see all commands. Run dox help <command> for one command.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
dart pub global activate dox 3.0.0-alpha.4

Add the pub bin folder to your PATH

If your shell can not find dox, add this line to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc, and open a new terminal:

export PATH="$PATH":"$HOME/.pub-cache/bin"

To remove the CLI:

dart pub global deactivate dox

docs.title: All commands
docs.text: Command What it does dox create <name> [--version <v>] create a new project dox serve (or dox s) start the dev server with build_runner watch dox build build the native (AOT) bundle into build/bundle dox build_runner:watch / dox build_runner:build run the code generator dox create:controller <name> [-r] [-ws] create a controller dox create:middleware <name> create a middleware dox create:dto <name> create a DTO (typed, checked input) dox create:serializer <name> create a serializer dox create:model <name> [-m] (or make:model) create a model, and with -m its migration dox make:migration <name> [--sql] (or create:migration) create a Dart migration, or a .sql one with --sql dox migration:run (or dox migrate) run new migrations dox migration:rollback [--step=N] undo the last batch, or the last N migrations dox migration:reset undo all migrations dox migration:refresh undo all, then run all again dox migration:status show which migrations ran, and their batch dox key:generate make a new APP_KEY dox env:generate make lib/config/env.dart (the typed env class) from .env.example, see Environment Variables dox env:check check the env against lib/config/env.dart. Prints every missing or bad key (exit code 1) dox openapi:generate [dir] write openapi.json and openapi.yaml (default storage/openapi), see OpenAPI dox update update the CLI dox version (or dox -v) show the CLI version dox help [command] show help

docs.title: Create a project
docs.text:
dox create new_blog
dox create new_blog --version v3.0.0-alpha.4

dox create copies the dox-sample template from GitHub. Without --version, it uses the latest release of the template.

docs.title: Run the dev server
docs.text:
dox serve                         # or: dox s
dox s --ignore-build-runner       # do not run build_runner watch

dox serve runs dart run bin/server.dart. When a .dart file changes, it restarts the server. It also runs build_runner watch, so generated files stay up to date.

docs.title: Run the code generator
docs.text:
dox build_runner:watch   # watch files and build again on each change
dox build_runner:build   # build once

docs.title: Build for production
docs.text:
dox build
cd build/bundle
./bin/server

dox build does these steps:

  1. It runs build_runner (when your app uses it).
  2. It runs dart build cli --target bin/server.dart --output build.
  3. It copies db/ and .env.example into build/bundle.

When a step fails, it stops with exit code 1, so CI can stop too. See Deployment.

docs.title: Make an app key
docs.text:
dox key:generate

It writes a new APP_KEY to your .env file.

docs.title: Controller
docs.text:
dox create:controller Blog       # default controller
dox create:controller Blog -r    # resource controller
dox create:controller Chat -ws   # WebSocket controller
  • A default or resource controller goes to lib/app/http/controllers/.
  • A WebSocket controller goes to lib/app/ws/controllers/. See WebSocket.
  • -r adds the methods index, create, store, show, edit, update and destroy.

File and class names

Word breaks are kept. dox create:controller BlogPost makes blog_post.controller.dart with the class BlogPostController. The same is true for middleware, DTOs and serializers.

docs.title: Middleware
docs.text: dox create:middleware Auth

docs.title: DTO
docs.text:
dox create:dto CreateBlog

It makes lib/app/http/dtos/create_blog.dto.dart. Then run dox build_runner:build. See Validation.

docs.title: Serializer
docs.text: dox create:serializer Blog

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
dox create:model Blog
dox create:model Blog -m   # also makes the create_blogs_table migration
  • -m (or --migration) makes a Dart migration create_<table>_table.
  • The table name is the model name in plural snake case: BlogPost makes blog_posts.
  • The model gets @DoxModel(table: 'blog_posts'), so it uses the same table.
  • make:model is the same command.

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
dox make:migration create_blogs_table          # .dart file (default)
dox make:migration create_blogs_table --sql    # .sql file

docs.title: Database settings
docs.text:
The migration commands read the database settings from the .env file:

.env
# postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
# for sqlite: the file path
DB_NAME=postgres
DB_USERNAME=admin
DB_PASSWORD=password
  • DB_CONNECTION is postgres, mysql or sqlite. The default is postgres.
  • The default port is 5432 for postgres and 3306 for mysql.
  • DB_DATABASE works too, in place of DB_NAME.
  • Put comments on their own line. A # after a value becomes part of the value.

.env or environment, not both

When a .env file exists, these commands read only the .env file. They use the real environment variables only when there is no .env file. This is different from Env.get(), where a real environment variable wins.

docs.title: Run migrations
docs.text:
dox migration:run    # or: dox migrate
dox migration:status

docs.title: Undo migrations
docs.text:
dox migration:rollback           # undo the last batch
dox migration:rollback --step=2  # undo the last 2 migrations
dox migration:reset              # undo all migrations
dox migration:refresh            # undo all migrations, then run them again

migrate:rollback, migrate:reset, migrate:refresh and migrate:status also work.

  • A failed migration stops the run, and the CLI exits with code 1.
  • On MySQL, statements like CREATE, ALTER and DROP save right away. So when a migration fails half way, these changes are not undone.

docs.title: Update the CLI
docs.text:
dox update runs dart pub global activate dox. This installs the latest stable version, not a preview. To stay on a preview version, run the install command with the version again:

dart pub global activate dox 3.0.0-alpha.4

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: Declare your env keys once, in a typed class. Then env.appPort is an int, your IDE suggests every key, and a missing key stops the app at startup.

docs.title: The typed env class
docs.text:
A new project already has lib/config/env.dart, with the keys the config files read. The list is in the Env reference.

This example class shows the kinds of getters you can write:

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'env.g.dart';

enum LogLevel { debug, info, error }

@DoxEnv()
abstract class AppEnv {
  static AppEnv load([EnvReader? reader]) {
    return _$AppEnv.load(reader);
  }

  String get appName;                       // APP_NAME, required
  String get appKey;                        // APP_KEY, required
  int get dbPort => 5432;                   // DB_PORT, default 5432
  bool get appDebug => false;               // APP_DEBUG, default false
  LogLevel get logLevel => LogLevel.info;   // LOG_LEVEL=debug
  Duration get cacheTtl => const Duration(minutes: 5); // CACHE_TTL=5m
  List<String> get corsOrigins => <String>[];          // CORS_ORIGINS=a.com,b.com

  @EnvKey('AWS_BUCKET')
  String? get s3Bucket;                     // optional, null when not set
}

/// The env of the app. Read and checked once, on first use.
final AppEnv env = AppEnv.load();

Run dart run build_runner build (or dox build_runner:build) after each change to the class. It writes env.g.dart.

Use it anywhere:

import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(port: env.dbPort /* int */, ...),
  },
);

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
• Key: the getter name in UPPER_SNAKE case. appName reads APP_NAME, s3Bucket reads S3_BUCKET. Use @EnvKey('X') for another name.
  • Default: the getter body. It can be any expression, like Platform.numberOfProcessors. It runs only when the key is missing. A default can not read another env getter.
  • Optional: a nullable getter with no body (String? get s3Bucket;). It is null when the key is missing.
  • Required: any other getter with no body. A missing key stops the app.
  • Empty: an empty value (or the text null) counts as missing.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Type Value in .env String any text int, double, num 3000, 0.5 bool true/false, 1/0, yes/no, on/off (any case) Uri https://dox.dev Duration a number and a unit: 500ms, 30s, 5m, 2h, 1d. A plain number is seconds: 300 is 5 minutes. an enum the name of a value, any case: debug List<String> comma separated: a, b, c. Empty items are dropped.

Any other type is a build error.

docs.title: Fail fast
docs.text:
AppEnv.load() reads every key one time. Then it checks them all, and throws one EnvException that lists every missing or bad key:

EnvException: the env is not valid
  - APP_KEY is missing
  - DB_PORT must be an int, not "abc"

The env variable is made on first use. The config files use it, so this happens when the app starts. After that, env.dbPort is a plain field read. There is no lookup and no parsing on each request.

docs.title: Where values come from
docs.text:
Dox reads values from two places:

  1. Real environment variables (set in the shell, Docker or systemd).
  2. The .env file in the folder where you start the app.

The environment wins

A real environment variable wins over the .env file. So you can keep .env for development and use real variables in production. The .env file is optional.

docs.title: The .env file
docs.text:
.env
APP_NAME=dox
APP_KEY=change-me
DB_PORT=5432
  • One KEY=value per line.
  • Dox removes all ", ' and ` characters from a value. So APP_NAME="My app" gives My app.
  • A = inside the value is kept: TOKEN=a=b gives a=b.
  • Put a comment on its own line. A # after a value is part of the value.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
dox env:generate   # make lib/config/env.dart from .env.example
dox env:check      # load the env and print every missing or bad key

dox env:generate reads .env.example:

  • digits become an int with that default: APP_PORT=3000 gives int get appPort => 3000;
  • true/false become a bool with that default
  • an empty value becomes an optional String?
  • any other value becomes a required String. The example value is never a default, so a secret in the example can not leak into the code.
  • # comment lines above a key become its doc comment

It does not overwrite an existing lib/config/env.dart. Run dox build_runner:build after it.

dox env:check loads AppEnv from lib/config/env.dart, with the real environment and .env. It exits with code 1 when a key is missing or bad. Use it in CI or before a deploy.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Pass your own values to load(). Nothing is read from the shell or .env:

AppEnv env = AppEnv.load(
  EnvReader(
    environment: <String, String>{'APP_KEY': 'test'},
    dotEnv: <String, String>{'DB_PORT': '5433'},
  ),
);

docs.title: Env.get: the low-level way
docs.text:
Env.get() reads one key by name. Use it for a key you only know at run time. For normal config, use the typed class.

Env.get<String>('APP_KEY');             // '' when missing
Env.get('APP_KEY', 'default_value');
Env.get<int>('APP_PORT', 3000);
Env.get<bool>('SOCKETIO_ENABLED', false); // true, 1, yes, on
Env.get<String?>('AWS_BUCKET');          // null when it is not set

A missing or empty key gives the default. With no default:

  • String gives an empty string ''. It is never the text "null".
  • String? and dynamic give null. With no type, like Env.get('KEY'), the type is dynamic, so you get null.
  • int, num, double and bool throw an ArgumentError with the key name. A value that is not a number throws too.

Env.get() looks up and converts the value on every call. Do not call it on a hot path.

APP_KEY

When APP_KEY is empty and APP_ENV=production, Dox().startServer() stops with an error. In other environments it logs a warning. Make a key with dox key:generate.

docs.title: File Storage
docs.text:
Storage() saves and reads files on a disk: the local folder, AWS S3 (and R2, MinIO, Spaces), or memory. It runs on dox_storage, which is built into dox_core.

Route.post('/avatar', (DoxRequest req) async {
  RequestFile file = req.input('avatar');
  String path = await Storage().putRequestFile('avatars', file);
  return <String, String>{'path': path}; // /avatars/<uuid>.png
});

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
Without a config, Dox has one disk: local, in the storage folder. To add disks, make lib/config/storage.dart:

lib/config/storage.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

StorageConfig storage = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'local': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'local',
      'root': 'storage',
      'url': 'https://app.test/files', // for url() and signedUrl()
    },
    's3': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 's3',
      'bucket': env.awsBucket,
      'region': env.awsDefaultRegion,
      'key': env.awsAccessKeyId,
      'secret': env.awsSecretAccessKey,
      'endpoint': env.awsEndpoint, // R2, MinIO, Spaces
    },
    'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
  },
);

The s3 disk reads five keys that a new project does not have yet. Add them to lib/config/env.dart and run dart run build_runner build. They are nullable, so the app still starts without them when you do not use S3:

lib/config/env.dart
  String? get awsBucket;

  String get awsDefaultRegion => 'us-east-1';

  String? get awsAccessKeyId;

  String? get awsSecretAccessKey;

  /// R2, MinIO or Spaces. Null for AWS.
  String? get awsEndpoint;

Then pass it to AppConfig(storage: storage) in lib/config/app.dart.

Driver Options local root (default storage), url, app_key (default: your APP_KEY), visibility s3 bucket, region, key, secret, token, endpoint, path_style (MinIO), url (CDN), visibility, acl, batch_delete memory none. For tests

The s3 disk needs bucket, key and secret. When one is missing, the first use of the disk throws an error.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
// save with a new uuid file name, returns '/images/<uuid>.png'
String path = await Storage().put('images', bytes, extension: 'png');
String path2 = await Storage().putRequestFile('images', file);

Uint8List? bytes = await Storage().get(path);  // null when missing
bool found = await Storage().exists(path);
await Storage().delete(path);

String url = await Storage().url(path);         // needs the disk `url` option
String signed = await Storage().signedUrl(path, expiresIn: Duration(minutes: 10));

// another disk
await Storage().disk('s3').put('reports', bytes, extension: 'pdf');

putRequestFile on the local disk moves the upload temp file. It does not read it into memory.

docs.title: stream and download
docs.text:
Route.get('/photo', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().stream(req.input('path'));    // shown in the browser
});

Route.get('/report', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().disk('s3').download('reports/2024.pdf'); // saved as a file
});

Both read the file as a stream, from any disk, with Content-Length. A big file is never loaded into memory. A missing file answers 404.

docs.title: Full disk API
docs.text: Storage().use('s3') returns the dox_storage Disk: copy, move, listAll, getMetaData, putStream, setVisibility and more. See dox_storage.

docs.title: Serve local signed URLs
docs.text:
// lib/routes/web.dart
Route.files('files');                    // GET /files/{key*}, signed URLs only
Route.files('public', signed: false);    // any file of the disk
Route.files('docs', disk: 'memory');     // another disk than the default

String url = await Storage().signedUrl('invoices/1.pdf'); // https://app.test/files/invoices/1.pdf?expires=...&signature=...

A missing, wrong or expired signature answers 403. Set the disk url option to the full URL of the route (https://app.test/files).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Dox().storage is the DriveManager that Storage() uses. fake(name) swaps a disk with an empty memory disk:

Disk fake = Dox().storage.fake('s3');
await uploadReport();
expect(await fake.exists('reports/2024.pdf'), isTrue);
Dox().storage.restore('s3');

Disk keys have no / at the start. See Testing.

docs.title: Your own driver
docs.text:
Implement DriverContract from package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart. Register it in a service, so every isolate has it:

Dox().storage.register('dropbox', DropboxDriver());
await Storage().disk('dropbox').put('notes', bytes, extension: 'txt');

docs.title: Isolate
docs.text: This page explains how Dox runs your app on many isolates (threads), and what that means for your code.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Dox starts many isolates. Each one runs its own HTTP server on the same port. The operating system spreads the connections between them.

  • Native server on Linux: each isolate has its own socket (SO_REUSEPORT).
  • Native server on macOS: the isolates share one socket.
  • Native server on Windows: only one isolate serves HTTP.
  • dart:io server: HttpServer.bind(..., shared: true) on every system.

With the native server, each isolate has its own Rust acceptor on the port:

flowchart TD
    OS["Port 3000<br>the OS spreads the connections"] --> A1["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A2["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A3["Rust acceptor"]
    A1 --> I1["Isolate 1, main<br>own DB pool, own memory cache"]
    A2 --> I2["Isolate 2<br>own DB pool, own memory cache"]
    A3 --> I3["Isolate N<br>own DB pool, own memory cache"]
    I2 -. "crash: started again after 1 second" .-> I2
    I1 -. "crash: the process exits" .-> S["Supervisor restarts the process<br>Docker, systemd"]

See Native server for the two servers.

docs.title: How many isolates
docs.text:
By default Dox starts one isolate per CPU core (Platform.numberOfProcessors). So one process uses the whole machine.

To change it, set totalIsolate in lib/config/app.dart. A new app reads it from APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  totalIsolate: env.appTotalIsolate ?? Platform.numberOfProcessors,
);

You can also set it in code, before startServer(). This wins over the config:

bin/server.dart
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().totalIsolate(2);
await Dox().startServer();

Use fewer isolates when:

  • the machine also runs the database or other heavy work, or
  • you use WebSocket rooms without the Redis adapter. A room only reaches clients on the same isolate. Use 1, or see WebSocket.

docs.title: Each isolate has its own memory
docs.text:
Isolates do not share memory. This has some effects on your code:

  • A static value or a singleton exists once per isolate. When you change it in one isolate, the others do not see it.
  • The memory cache store is per isolate. Use the redis store to share cache data. See Cache.
  • To share data between isolates or servers, use a database, Redis or files.

Dox().isolateId tells you which isolate runs the code. The first isolate is 1.

docs.title: What each isolate does at start
docs.text:
Dox copies the AppConfig, the services and the routes you added before startServer() to each new isolate. Then every isolate:

  1. runs setup() of each service (for example, it opens its own database pool),
  2. registers the routes of your routers,
  3. reads the parameter types of each controller once,
  4. starts its HTTP server.

This happens once at start, not on each request.

Because the config and services are copied, they must not hold open sockets or database pools. Open these in setup(). See Services.

docs.title: When an isolate crashes
docs.text:
• An error in a request is caught. Dox sends a 500 and keeps going.
  • An async error outside a request (for example a future that nobody awaits) is caught and passed to errorHandler. The isolate keeps running.
  • If a worker isolate still dies, Dox prints [dox] isolate N exited, restarting to stderr. It starts a new isolate after 1 second.
  • If the first (main) isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. Let a supervisor start it again, like Docker restart: or systemd Restart=always. See Deployment.

docs.title: Native server
docs.text:
Dox runs on a native HTTP server by default. It comes from the package dox_http_native. You do not need to set anything.

  • Rust (hyper) owns the sockets and parses HTTP.
  • All your code stays in Dart: routes, controllers, DTOs, middleware, ORM.
  • It is much faster than the dart:io server. In a hello world test on one core it served about 5 times more requests. See Performance.

You do not need Rust. The package downloads a ready-built library for your system when you build the app.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Rust reads the requests from the sockets.
  2. It sends the requests to Dart in batches (one message per batch).
  3. Dart runs your handlers, like before.
  4. Dart sends all answers back to Rust in one call.

The native server has the same API as the dart:io HttpServer. So req.httpRequest, HttpResponse and code written for dart:io keep working.

Each isolate runs its own server on the same port:

  • Linux: one socket per isolate (SO_REUSEPORT). The kernel spreads the connections.
  • macOS: the isolates share one socket.
  • Windows: only one isolate serves HTTP.

docs.title: Use dart:io instead
docs.text:
Set server in AppConfig:

AppConfig(
  // ...
  server: ServerBackend.dartIo,
);

Or set the env var DOX_SERVER=dartio. The env var wins over the config.

Dox also uses dart:io by itself in these cases:

  • The native library did not load. Dox prints one warning line at start: [dox] warning: dox_http_native did not load, using the dart:io server (...).
  • The app has WebSocket or Socket.IO routes. The native server can not upgrade a connection to WebSocket yet.

DOX_SERVER=native forces the native server, also for an app with WebSocket routes. WebSocket upgrades then fail with 500. Socket.IO long-polling works.

Each isolate has its own Rust network thread. DOX_HTTP_THREAD=shared puts all isolates on one thread. It is off by default: on 2 cores the one thread was the limit and req/s fell by a quarter. Leave it off unless you measure a gain.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Max size of the request line plus headers: 16 KB. Bigger gets 431.
  • A bad request gets 400.
  • A body over the bigger of maxBodySize and maxMultipartSize gets 413 from Rust. Each body type is checked again in Dart with its own limit.
  • A response is sent when it is closed. It is kept in memory until then, also a big file. Use a proxy (nginx, Caddy) or a storage link for big downloads.
  • No WebSocket upgrade yet (see above).
  • compress: true works: Dart gzips the body.

docs.title: Where the library comes from
docs.text:
The build hook of dox_http_native (hook/build.dart) picks the first one that works:

  1. A path you give in the root pubspec.yaml of your app:

    hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_http_native:
      lib_path: /path/to/libdox_http_native.so

  2. A local build in native/target/release of the package (for work on Dox itself).

  3. The ready-built library from the GitHub release, checked with sha256. There are builds for macOS (arm64, x64), Linux (x64, arm64) and Windows (x64).
  4. A build from source with cargo, when Rust is installed.

When none works, the app still builds and runs on dart:io.

Use dart build cli

dart compile exe does not run build hooks. Use dox build or dart build cli. See Deployment.

docs.title: Work on the native code
docs.text:
The Rust code is in packages/dox-http-native/native.

cd packages/dox-http-native/native
cargo build --release   # the hook uses this build from now on
cargo test
cd .. && dart test --concurrency=1

To make a release of the libraries, push a tag like dox_http_native-v3.0.0-alpha.4. The version in the tag must be the version in packages/dox-http-native/pubspec.yaml, because the build hook downloads from the tag of its own version.

The Native workflow builds the 5 libraries and uploads them with a SHA256SUMS file. Copy the hashes into _sha256 in hook/build.dart before you publish the package.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
This page shows how fast Dox is, and how to keep your app fast in production.

The short version:

  1. Build with dox build and run the AOT binary. Never dart run in production.
  2. Put Caddy or nginx in front for HTTPS and gzip.
  3. Keep the default isolates (one per CPU core).
  4. Keep the body limits on. Uploads stream to disk.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text:
A "hello world" test. Each server answers GET / with the plain text Hello World. Dox is a small real Dox app with one route.

Hello world only measures framework overhead. A real app spends most of its time on the database, JSON and your own code, so the gaps are much smaller there.

docs.title: 1 core
docs.text:
Server req/s p99 ms CPU % peak MB Dox, native server 171,042 0.92 100 9 Dox, dart:io server 33,154 5.48 101 39 Bun 1.4.3 181,162 1.13 101 14 Node 24.22.0 81,909 2.26 101 54 Pure Rust hyper (the ceiling) 254,349 0.47 100 5

On one core, Dox with the native server is about as fast as Bun (0.94x). It is 5x faster than Dox on dart:io.

How it was run:

  • Docker on an Apple M2 (8 CPUs in the Docker VM), linux/arm64.
  • The server and wrk run in two containers, pinned to different CPUs: server on CPU 0, wrk on CPUs 2-7.
  • wrk 4.2.0, 100 connections (the tables) and 256 connections. 5 seconds warm-up, then 3 runs of 10 seconds. The tables show the median.
  • CPU % and peak memory come from docker stats. 100% = one core.
  • Dart 3.13.6, Rust 1.99.1. Dox is built with dart build cli (this is what dox build does). The build hook of dox_http_native builds the Rust library with cargo.
  • DOX_SERVER=dartio runs the same Dox app on dart:io.

docs.title: App benchmark
docs.text: A small real app, the same in each language: GET /json returns a map, GET /db reads one row by id from Postgres, GET /queries?n=20 reads 20 rows one after another. The table has 10,000 rows. Each server runs alone on one or two pinned CPUs, Postgres 18 and wrk on other CPUs, 256 connections, 4 database connections per core, 3 runs of 10 seconds, median. Versions: Dox 3.0.0-alpha.3 (native server, dox_postgres_native), Go 1.27 (net/http + pgx), Bun 1.4 (Bun.serve + Bun.sql), Node 24 (node:http + pg), dart:io (HttpServer + package:postgres).

docs.title: 1 core
docs.text:
1 core: 1.5× Bun, 2.3× Go

GET /db: read one row from Postgres. Requests per second, higher is better.

req/s p99 RAM Doxnative server + driver 85,381fastest 5.65 ms 24 MB BunBun.serve + Bun.sql 57,6141.5× slower 6.11 ms 36 MB Gonet/http + pgx 36,7062.3× slower 14.49 ms 18 MB dart:io+ package:postgres 12,1467.0× slower 47.62 ms 62 MB

Dox 3.0.0-alpha.3 · Bun 1.4 · Go 1.27 · Dart 3.13 · Postgres 18 · 256 connections · wrk · median of 3 runs

Route Dox Bun Go dart:io /json req/s 157,036 176,148 79,884 33,670 /db req/s 85,381 57,614 36,706 12,146 /queries req/s 9,745 10,097 3,810 966 /db p99 ms 5.65 6.11 14.49 47.62 /db peak MB 24 36 18 62

docs.title: 2 cores
docs.text:
2 cores: still the fastest

GET /db on 2 CPU cores. Dox runs one isolate per core; Bun and Node one worker process per core.

req/s p99 RAM Dox2 isolates 138,514fastest 3.62 ms 51 MB Bun2 workers 128,9981.1× slower 5.61 ms 57 MB Node2 workers + pg 61,6112.2× slower 8.06 ms 297 MB Gonet/http + pgx 49,3932.8× slower 8.53 ms 22 MB

Dox 3.0.0-alpha.3 · Bun 1.4 · Go 1.27 · Node 24 · Postgres 18 · 256 connections · wrk · median of 3 runs

2 cores: 20 queries per request

GET /queries?n=20: 20 reads from Postgres, one after another, in one request.

req/s Dox2 isolates 12,902fastest Bun2 workers 11,0061.2× slower Node2 workers + pg 5,8702.2× slower Gonet/http + pgx 5,1342.5× slower

Dox 3.0.0-alpha.3 · Bun 1.4 · Go 1.27 · Node 24 · Postgres 18 · 256 connections · wrk · median of 3 runs

Route Dox Bun Go Node /json req/s 251,427 385,553 175,009 156,389 /db req/s 138,514 128,998 49,393 61,611 /queries req/s 12,902 11,006 5,134 5,870 /db p99 ms 3.62 5.61 8.53 8.06 /db peak MB 51 57 22 297

Dox runs one isolate per core, Bun and Node one worker process per core. On the database routes Dox is ahead of all of them on 2 cores, and its p99 is the lowest. On /json Bun is faster: its server is C++ and calls the JavaScript handler on the same thread, while Dox hands each batch of requests from the Rust thread to the Dart isolate.

Dox on dart:io with the Dart postgres driver is 4 to 10 times slower than Dox with the native server and driver. Keep both on.

docs.title: Dart VM flags
docs.text: We tried a bigger young generation (DART_VM_OPTIONS=--new_gen_semi_max_size=64 and 128) for a better p99. Over 5 runs the change was inside the noise, and memory did not move. So there is no flag to set. Dox never sets VM flags for you. DART_VM_OPTIONS is read by the AOT binary from dox build, so you can try your own.

docs.title: Request body limits
docs.text:
Dox reads a body while it streams in, and stops once it is too big. It answers 413 Payload Too Large. It checks Content-Length first, so a big upload is refused before one byte is read. It also counts bytes while reading, so a client that sends no Content-Length (chunked) is stopped too.

AppConfig(
  maxBodySize: 10 * 1024 * 1024,        // JSON and urlencoded, default 10 MB
  maxMultipartSize: 100 * 1024 * 1024,  // form-data uploads, default 100 MB
);

Set the same limit in the proxy (client_max_body_size in nginx).

docs.title: File uploads
docs.text:
• A file up to 1 MB stays in memory.
  • A bigger file is written to a temp file while it arrives. So a big upload does not fill the memory.
  • The temp file is deleted when the response is done. So save it before you return from the controller.
RequestFile file = req.input('video');

file.length;          // size in bytes
await file.size;      // size in KB
file.stream();        // read it in chunks
await file.store('videos');           // to storage (a cheap move on local disk)
await file.moveTo('/data/videos/1.mp4');
await file.bytes;     // whole file in memory. avoid for big files

docs.title: Big responses
docs.text:
Return a Stream<List<int>> or a File. Dox pipes it to the client and does not load it all into memory.

Route.get('/video', (DoxRequest req) => File('storage/video.mp4'));

A File response sets Content-Type (from the file name), Content-Length and Accept-Ranges. It answers Range: bytes=... with 206 Partial Content, so video players can seek and downloads can resume.

Storage().stream() and Storage().download() on the local disk also stream the file and send Content-Length.

JSON and text responses are encoded once, straight to bytes, with Content-Length set.

docs.title: gzip
docs.text:
gzip in Dart is off by default.

AppConfig(compress: true);
  • It saves bandwidth, but costs CPU on every response, in the same isolate that serves requests.
  • A proxy (Caddy, nginx) does it better. Turn it on in Dart only when there is no proxy.
  • With compress: true, text and JSON responses are sent chunked, without Content-Length, because dart:io only gzips when the length is not set.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
LogMiddleware prints one JSON line per request. Writing to stdout blocks the isolate. So Dox collects log lines and writes them every 20 ms (or every 64 KB) in one write. If the process is killed hard, the last 20 ms of request logs can be lost. Errors from Logger are still written right away.

Turn LogMiddleware off when a proxy already writes access logs.

docs.title: What Dox does for you
docs.text:
• Routes are grouped by method. The regex of each route is built once, not on every request.
  • The argument types of each controller are read once at start, not on every request.

docs.title: Services
docs.text: A service is a class with a setup() method. Dox runs it at start, in every isolate. Use it to set up things like the database, auth or WebSocket.

docs.title: Why services
docs.text:
Dox runs your app on many isolates (see Isolate). Each isolate has its own memory.

So code that you run once in bin/server.dart only sets up the first isolate. The other isolates do not see it. For example, they have no database connection.

A service fixes this. Dox sends the list of services to each isolate, and each isolate runs setup() itself.

docs.title: Create a service
docs.text:
Implement DoxService and put your code in setup(). setup() can be async. Dox waits for it.

lib/services/orm_service.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMService implements DoxService {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }
}

docs.title: Register it
docs.text:
Add an instance of the service to the list in lib/config/services.dart:

lib/config/services.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/services/auth_service.dart';
import 'package:my_app/services/orm_service.dart';

List<DoxService> services = <DoxService>[
  ORMService(),
  AuthService(),
];

This list goes to AppConfig(services: services) in lib/config/app.dart.

You can also add a service in code, before startServer():

bin/server.dart
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().addService(MyService());
await Dox().startServer();

docs.title: Example: auth
When setup() runs
docs.text:
In each isolate, Dox does these steps in this order:

  1. It runs setup() of each service, one after the other, in list order.
  2. It registers the routes of your routers.
  3. It starts the HTTP server.

So routes can use what a service set up. For example, Route.websocket() needs the WebSocket service to run first.

dox openapi:generate also runs setup() of every service, because it needs the routes.

docs.title: Rules for a service
docs.text:
• Open connections in setup(), not in the constructor. Dox copies the service object to each isolate. An open socket or database pool can not be copied, so the isolate fails to start.
  • Keep setup() short. It runs once per isolate. Data you load in it is kept once per isolate, so 8 isolates keep 8 copies.
  • Do not depend on another isolate. Each isolate has its own static values and singletons. To share data between isolates, use a database, Redis or the cache with the redis driver.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: This page shows how to test a Dox app with the test package: HTTP routes, cache, storage, env and the database.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add the test packages as dev dependencies:

dart pub add dev:test dev:http

Put your tests in the test/ folder. Run them with:

dart test

docs.title: Test HTTP routes
docs.text:
Start the real server once for the whole file. Then send requests to it with package:http.

test/http_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

String baseUrl = 'http://localhost:${appConfig.serverPort}';

void main() {
  setUpAll(() async {
    Dox().initialize(appConfig);
    Dox().totalIsolate(1);
    await Dox().startServer();
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await Dox().server.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/ping', () async {
    http.Response response = await http.get(Uri.parse('$baseUrl/api/ping'));
    expect(response.statusCode, 200);
    expect(response.body, 'pong');
  });
}
  • startServer() returns when the server listens. You do not need to wait after it.
  • Dox().totalIsolate(1) runs the server on one isolate. By default Dox starts one isolate per CPU core. A test does not need them, and they make the start slower.
  • With one isolate, you can also add a route inside a test with Route.get(...). It works right away.
  • Do not run dox serve on the same port while you test. The test can fail to start, or send its requests to the dev server. Stop dox serve, or use another APP_PORT for tests.

docs.title: Test the cache
docs.text:
Dox().cache is the CacheManager that Cache() uses. Replace it with a memory store, so tests do not write files or need Redis:

setUp(() {
  Dox().cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(
    defaultStore: 'memory',
    stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
      'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
    },
  ));
});

test('caches the posts', () async {
  await Cache().put('posts', <String>['a', 'b']);
  expect(await Cache().get('posts'), <dynamic>['a', 'b']);
});

A new CacheManager in setUp gives each test an empty cache. See Cache.

docs.title: Test file storage
docs.text:
Dox().storage.fake(name) swaps one disk with an empty memory disk. restore(name) puts the real disk back.

setUpAll(() {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
});

test('saves the report', () async {
  Disk fake = Dox().storage.fake('s3');

  String path = await Storage()
      .disk('s3')
      .put('reports', <int>[1, 2, 3], extension: 'pdf'); // '/reports/<uuid>.pdf'

  expect(await fake.exists(path.substring(1)), isTrue);
  Dox().storage.restore('s3');
});
  • Call Dox().initialize() first. The storage disks are made from appConfig.
  • Storage() paths start with /. A Disk key does not, so remove the first / when you ask the Disk directly.

See File Storage.

docs.title: Test the env
docs.text:
Pass your own values to AppEnv.load(). Then nothing is read from the shell or the .env file:

AppEnv env = AppEnv.load(
  EnvReader(
    environment: <String, String>{'APP_KEY': 'test'},
    dotEnv: <String, String>{'DB_PORT': '5433'},
  ),
);
expect(env.dbPort, 5433);

A missing or bad key throws an EnvException. So you can also test that your app stops on a bad env. See Environment Variables.
