docs.title: Test the database
docs.text:
A test that uses models needs a real database. Run the migrations and the ORM service once, before the tests:

test/db_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:my_app/services/orm_service.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  setUpAll(() async {
    Dox().initialize(appConfig);
    await Migrator(
      connection: await databaseConfig
          .getConnectionConfig()
          .getDatabaseConnection(),
    ).migrate();
    await ORMService().setup();
  });

  test('saves a user', () async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = 'Dox'
      ..email = 'test-${DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch}@dox.dev'
      ..password = 'secret';
    await user.save();
    expect(user.id, isNotNull);
  });
}
  • Use a separate test database. Set its name in the env of the test run, for example DB_NAME=app_test dart test.
  • Make each test data unique (like the email above), or delete it at the end of the test. Then tests do not break each other.
  • ORMService().setup() runs the same code as at server start. See Services.

Run test files one by one

dart test runs test files at the same time. When two files start the server on the same port, or use the same tables, run them one by one: dart test --concurrency=1.

docs.title: WebSocket
docs.text:
dox_websocket adds WebSocket routes to a Dox app. Use it for live chat, notifications and other real-time updates.

Want Socket.IO clients?

Use Socket.IO. Turn it on with AppConfig(socketIo: SocketIoConfig(enabled: true)). It runs on the same port, works with the official Socket.IO clients, and has acks and namespaces. dox_websocket keeps working next to it.

WebSocket uses the dart:io server

The native server can not upgrade a connection to WebSocket yet. So when your app has a WebSocket route, Dox uses the dart:io server by itself. See Native server.

docs.title: 1. Add the package
docs.text: dart pub add dox_websocket:^3.0.0-alpha.4

docs.title: 2. Create a WebSocket service
docs.text: The service creates the WebSocket server in every isolate. See Services.

docs.title: Many isolates (Redis)
docs.text:
Pick this for production. It works with more than one isolate and more than one server.

lib/services/websocket_service.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_websocket/dox_websocket.dart';
import 'package:ioredis/ioredis.dart';

class WebsocketService implements DoxService {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Redis sub = Redis(RedisOptions(host: env.redisHost));
    Redis pub = sub.duplicate();

    WebsocketServer io = WebsocketServer(Dox());
    io.adapter(WebsocketRedisAdapter(subscriber: sub, publisher: pub));
  }
}

Add ioredis ^2.0.0-alpha.2 to your pubspec.yaml.

docs.title: One isolate
docs.text:
Pick this for a small app or for local work, when you do not want Redis.

lib/services/websocket_service.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_websocket/dox_websocket.dart';

class WebsocketService implements DoxService {
  @override
  void setup() {
    WebsocketServer(Dox());
  }
}

Set totalIsolate: 1 in lib/config/app.dart (or APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE=1).

Many isolates need Redis

Dox runs one isolate per CPU core by default. Each isolate has its own memory. Without an adapter, a message only reaches clients on the same isolate. The Redis adapter sends each message to all isolates and all servers.

docs.title: 3. Register the service
4. Create a controller
docs.text:
dox create:controller Chat -ws

This makes lib/app/ws/controllers/chat.controller.dart. Each method gets the WebsocketEmitter and the message from the client:

lib/app/ws/controllers/chat.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_websocket/dox_websocket.dart';

class ChatController {
  void intro(WebsocketEmitter emitter, dynamic message) {
    // send to the 'chat' room, but not to the sender
    emitter.room('chat').emitExceptSender('intro', message);
  }

  void noti(WebsocketEmitter emitter, dynamic message) {
    // send to the 'chat' room, also to the sender
    emitter.room('chat').emit('noti', message);
  }
}

A WebSocket connection stays open. So a controller method does not need to return a value.

docs.title: 5. Add the route
docs.text:
Use Route.websocket(path, callback). In the callback, map each event name to a controller method:

lib/routes/web.dart
ChatController chat = ChatController();

Route.websocket('ws', (WebsocketEvent event) {
  // the client sends event `intro`: run chat.intro
  event.on('intro', chat.intro);
  event.on('noti', chat.noti);
});

The URL is ws://127.0.0.1:{port}/ws. You can add more WebSocket routes on other paths. Route.websocket also takes middleware:, like other routes.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Client and server send JSON text.

The client sends event and message:

{"event": "intro", "message": "Mingalaba!"}

The server sends event, message, sender (the socket id of the sender) and room:

{"event": "intro", "message": "Mingalaba!", "sender": "ws:4f1c...", "room": "chat"}

Two events are built in:

Event Direction What it does connected server to client sent once after connect. message is {"id": "<socket id>"} joinRoom client to server joins the room. message is the room name

Each client is also in a room for its route, so emitter.emit() with no room reaches all clients of the same route.

docs.title: Dart
docs.text:
Use WebSocket from dart:io.

import 'dart:convert';
import 'dart:io';

void main() async {
  WebSocket socket = await WebSocket.connect('ws://localhost:3000/ws');

  socket.listen((dynamic data) {
    Map<String, dynamic> payload = jsonDecode(data as String);
    print('${payload['event']}: ${payload['message']}');
  });

  // join the chat room
  socket.add(jsonEncode(<String, dynamic>{
    'event': 'joinRoom',
    'message': 'chat',
  }));

  // send the intro event
  socket.add(jsonEncode(<String, dynamic>{
    'event': 'intro',
    'message': 'Mingalaba!',
  }));
}

docs.title: JavaScript
docs.text:
Use the browser WebSocket, or the client @dartondox/websocket:

import DoxWebsocket from '@dartondox/websocket';

const socket = DoxWebsocket('ws://127.0.0.1:3000/ws', {
  maxRetries: 18,
  retryAfter: 2000,
});

socket.onConnected(() => console.log(socket.id));
socket.onError(() => console.log('socket error'));
socket.onClose(() => console.log('socket closed'));

// listen for the intro event from the server
socket.on('intro', (msg) => console.log(msg));

// send the intro event
socket.emit('intro', 'Mingalaba!');

docs.title: room
docs.text:
Pick the room to send to. Use the same name the client sent with joinRoom.

emitter.room('chat').emit('event-name', message);

room() returns a new emitter. The room does not stay set for later events.

docs.title: emit
docs.text:
Send to every client in the room. Without room(), this is every client of the same route.

emitter.emit('event-name', message);

docs.title: emitExceptSender
docs.text:
Send to every client in the room, but not to the sender.

emitter.emitExceptSender('event-name', message);

docs.title: emitToSender
docs.text:
Send only to the client that sent the event.

emitter.emitToSender('event-name', message);

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Each guide solves one job from start to end. Copy the files, run the commands, and check the result. The reference pages explain each part in more detail. The guides link to them.

The code of all guides is in one app on GitHub: examples/guides. CI builds it and runs its tests on every push, so the code on these pages keeps working.

Guide What you get File upload Accept an image, check its size and type, save it, return its URL. Pagination A list route with page and per_page, and the JSON shape it returns. JWT authentication Register, log in, protect routes, read the user, log out. Custom errors Your own exception classes, one JSON shape for every error, logging. Background work Run work after the response, use another thread for CPU work, run a timer. Docker A small production image with dox build, Postgres, env and a health check. Testing with a database Tests on SQLite or a test Postgres, with migrations and cleanup. Static files and SPA Serve a folder or a single page app, with cache headers. CORS for a browser front-end The CORS setup that works with a React, Vue or Flutter web app. Environments Dev, staging and production config, .env files, secrets and APP_KEY.

All guides use the app that dox create my_app makes. The package name is my_app. Change it to your own package name in the imports.

docs.title: API docs with OpenAPI
docs.text: Your API gets docs for free. Turn on OpenAPI for the blog API, open the docs page, and make the docs better with a few comments and annotations.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app.
  • build_runner and dox_builder. A new app has both.

You do not add a package. dox_core already has dox_openapi in it.

docs.title: 1. Write the config
docs.text:
dox_builder already writes lib/openapi.g.dart when you run build_runner. It holds openApiRegistry: what the builder found in your routes, controllers, DTOs and models. Pass it to an OpenApiConfig:

lib/config/openapi.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:blog/openapi.g.dart';

OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
  info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
  registry: openApiRegistry,
);

Add it to AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:blog/config/openapi.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  /// OpenAPI docs (config/openapi.dart)
  openApi: openApi,
);

docs.title: 2. Build and start
docs.text:
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

.env has APP_ENV=development, so the docs routes are on.

docs.title: 3. Open the docs page
docs.text:
Open http://localhost:3000/docs in a browser. It is a Scalar page. It lists every route, with "Try it" buttons. It loads Scalar from the jsDelivr CDN and reads /openapi.json.

The app now has three new routes:

Route What it gives GET /docs the Scalar docs page (HTML) GET /openapi.json the OpenAPI 3.1 document as JSON GET /openapi.yaml the same document as YAML

docs.title: 4. Read the JSON
docs.text:
curl http://localhost:3000/openapi.json

This is the real output for the blog API, shortened. The top level:

{
  "openapi": "3.1.0",
  "info": {"title": "Blog API", "version": "1.0.0"},
  "paths": {
    "/ping": {},
    "/api/ping": {},
    "/api/posts": {},
    "/api/posts/{id}": {},
    "/api/auth/register": {},
    "/api/auth/login": {},
    "/api/auth/user": {}
  },
  "components": {
    "schemas": {"Post": {}, "SavePost": {}, "RegisterUser": {}, "LoginUser": {}, "User": {}, "ValidationError": {}},
    "securitySchemes": {
      "bearerAuth": {"type": "http", "scheme": "bearer", "bearerFormat": "JWT"}
    }
  }
}

POST /api/posts, as the builder found it. You wrote no docs code for it:

{
  "tags": ["Post"],
  "summary": "POST /api/posts",
  "operationId": "PostController.store",
  "requestBody": {
    "required": true,
    "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/SavePost"}}}
  },
  "responses": {
    "200": {"description": "Successful response"},
    "401": {"description": "Not logged in"},
    "422": {
      "description": "Validation failed",
      "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/ValidationError"}}}
    },
    "500": {"description": "Server error"}
  },
  "security": [{"bearerAuth": []}]
}

Where each part comes from:

Part Comes from tags: ["Post"] the class name PostController, without Controller summary the first line of the /// comment: /// POST /api/posts requestBody the argument SavePost body of store 401 and bearerAuth AuthMiddleware on the route 422 the route has a request class 200 with no body store returns DoxResponse, so the builder can not see the body. Step 6 fixes this

docs.title: 5. See how a DTO becomes a schema
docs.text:
This is the SavePost DTO of the tutorial:

lib/app/http/dtos/save_post.dto.dart
@Dto()
class SavePost {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 100)
  final String title;

  @Trim()
  @MinLength(10)
  final String body;

  const SavePost({required this.title, required this.body});

  static const DtoSchema<SavePost> schema = $SavePostDto;
}

And this is its schema in /openapi.json:

"SavePost": {
  "type": "object",
  "title": "SavePost",
  "properties": {
    "title": {"type": "string", "minLength": 3, "maxLength": 100},
    "body": {"type": "string", "minLength": 10}
  },
  "required": ["title", "body"]
}
In the DTO In the schema String title (not nullable) "type": "string" and title in required @Length(min: 3, max: 100) "minLength": 3, "maxLength": 100 @MinLength(10) "minLength": 10 @Email() (in RegisterUser) "format": "email" @Trim(), @Lowercase(), @Unique(...) nothing. They change or check the value on the server only

A model becomes a schema too. Post has id, the @Column fields title and body, and created_at and updated_at. Keys in hidden are left out. That is why User has no password.

The docs and the validation come from the same DTO. When you change a rule, run build_runner again, and the docs change with it.

docs.title: 6. Make the docs better
docs.text:
Write a /// comment on a controller method. The first line is the summary. The rest is the description. Add @Tags and @Response when the automatic result is not what you want. They come from dox_core, so there is no new import.

lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
class PostController {
  /// List all posts
  ///
  /// Newest posts are not first. There is no paging yet.
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  /// Create a post
  @Tags(<String>['Posts'])
  @Response(201, Post, description: 'The new post')
  Future<DoxResponse> store(SavePost body) async {
    Post post = Post()
      ..title = body.title
      ..body = body.body;
    await post.save();
    return response(post).statusCode(201);
  }

  // ...
}

Run dart run build_runner build again and restart the app. The real result:

"get": {
  "tags": ["Post"],
  "summary": "List all posts",
  "description": "Newest posts are not first. There is no paging yet.",
  "operationId": "PostController.index"
},
"post": {
  "tags": ["Posts"],
  "summary": "Create a post",
  "operationId": "PostController.store",
  "responses": {
    "201": {
      "description": "The new post",
      "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/Post"}}}
    },
    "401": {},
    "422": {},
    "500": {}
  }
}
  • @Response(201, Post) replaces the empty 200. The docs now match the real status code.
  • @Tags(['Posts']) moves the route to the group "Posts" in the docs page.
  • @Summary('...') and @Description('...') set the text without a /// comment.
  • @ApiIgnore() leaves a method (or a whole controller) out of the docs.

See OpenAPI: change the docs for all annotations.

docs.title: 7. Turn it off in production
docs.text:
You do not need to do anything. enabled is null by default. Then the docs routes are on only when APP_ENV is development or local.

With APP_ENV=production all three routes give 404:

curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000/docs           # 404
curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000/openapi.json   # 404

To show the docs on staging too, but never in production, set enabled yourself:

lib/config/openapi.dart
OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
  enabled: env.appEnv != 'production',
  info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
  registry: openApiRegistry,
);

Warning

enabled: true in production shows every route of your API to anyone. Only do it for a public API.

To give the document to a front-end team without a running server, write it to files with dox openapi:generate. See OpenAPI: write the files.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
curl -s http://localhost:3000/openapi.json | head -n 5

{
  "openapi": "3.1.0",
  "info": {
    "title": "Blog API",
    "version": "1.0.0"

Open http://localhost:3000/docs, find "Create a post" under "Posts", and send a request with "Try it".

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• OpenAPI for all options, the Scalar look, Swagger UI and login schemes
  • Validation rules for the rules and their JSON Schema keys
  • Environments for APP_ENV

docs.title: Background work
docs.text: Answer the request now and do the slow work after. Use another thread for CPU work. Run a job on a timer.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app.

docs.title: What Dox gives you
docs.text:
Dox has no job queue. It has three building blocks from Dart itself:

You want Use Runs where I/O work after the response (send an email, call an API, write rows) a Future you do not await the same isolate, between requests CPU work (resize an image, parse a big file, compute) Isolate.run() a new thread work every N minutes (cleanup, sync) Timer.periodic in a service one isolate of your choice

None of them survive a restart. See When you need a real queue.

docs.title: 1. Work after the response
docs.text:
Start the future and return. unawaited tells the linter you did this on purpose. An error in the future goes to the errorHandler of AppConfig. The isolate keeps running.

lib/app/http/controllers/report.controller.dart
import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:isolate';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ReportController {
  /// POST /api/reports
  /// Answers at once. The work runs after the response, in this isolate.
  Map<String, String> store(DoxRequest req) {
    String id = DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch.toString();
    unawaited(_build(id));
    return <String, String>{'id': id, 'status': 'queued'};
  }

  /// I/O work (database, HTTP calls, email) is fine here. It shares the
  /// event loop with the requests, so it must not block the CPU.
  Future<void> _build(String id) async {
    await Future<void>.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 2));
    print('report $id is ready');
  }

  /// GET /api/primes/{limit}
  /// CPU work runs on another thread with `Isolate.run`.
  /// The request waits for the result, but other requests are not blocked.
  Future<Map<String, int>> primes(int limit) async {
    int count = await Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(limit));
    return <String, int>{'limit': limit, 'primes': count};
  }
}

/// Must be a top level or static function with plain arguments.
/// The new isolate has no Dox, no database and no services.
int countPrimes(int limit) {
  List<bool> sieve = List<bool>.filled(limit + 1, true);
  int count = 0;
  for (int i = 2; i <= limit; i++) {
    if (!sieve[i]) continue;
    count++;
    for (int j = i * i; j <= limit; j += i) {
      sieve[j] = false;
    }
  }
  return count;
}

ReportController reportController = ReportController();

Do not block the event loop

_build runs on the same thread as the HTTP requests of this isolate. await on the database or on HTTP is fine. A long loop is not. Every request on this isolate waits for it. Put a long loop in Isolate.run.

docs.title: 2. CPU work on another thread
docs.text:
Isolate.run starts a new isolate, runs the function, and sends the result back. The function only gets what you pass in. It has no Dox(), no models and no Storage(). So pass plain data in (an int, a String, bytes), get plain data out, and save the result in the request isolate.

Both patterns are in the controller above: primes waits for the result. To not wait, combine them:

unawaited(Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(limit)).then(saveResult));

docs.title: 3. Work on a timer
docs.text:
setup() of a service runs in every isolate. Dox starts one per CPU core. So start the timer on isolate 1 only. Otherwise 8 isolates run the same cleanup.

lib/services/cleanup_service.dart
import 'dart:async';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

/// Work on a timer. `setup()` runs in every isolate, so the timer is
/// started on isolate 1 only. Otherwise 8 isolates do the same job.
class CleanupService implements DoxService {
  @override
  void setup() {
    if (Dox().isolateId != 1) return;
    Timer.periodic(const Duration(hours: 1), _run);
  }

  Future<void> _run(Timer timer) async {
    DateTime limit = DateTime.now().subtract(const Duration(days: 30));
    List<User> old = await User()
        .withTrash()
        .where('deleted_at', '<', limit)
        .get();
    for (User user in old) {
      await user.forceDelete();
    }
    print('cleanup: removed ${old.length} users');
  }
}
lib/config/services.dart
List<DoxService> services = <DoxService>[
  ORMService(),
  CleanupService(), // after ORMService, so the database is ready
];

When you run more than one process (two machines), each process has an isolate 1. Then the job runs twice. Use a database lock, or run the job from one place only.

docs.title: 4. Add the routes
Check it
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/reports

The answer comes at once:

{"id":"1792677668393002","status":"queued"}

Two seconds later, the server prints report 1792677668393002 is ready.

curl http://localhost:3000/api/primes/100000

{"limit":100000,"primes":9592}

docs.title: When you need a real queue
docs.text: The work above is lost when the process stops, and it does not retry. When that is not OK (payments, emails that must arrive), save the job as a row in a table first. Then a Timer.periodic service, or a second small Dart program, reads the table, does the work, and marks the row as done. A failed row stays in the table, so you can retry it. This is a queue with one extra table and no new service.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Isolate for what each isolate shares, and what it does not
  • Services
  • Custom errors for the errorHandler that gets the errors of a future nobody awaits

docs.title: CORS for a browser front-end
docs.text: Let a web app on another origin (http://localhost:5173 in development, https://my.app in production) call your API.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app.
  • A front-end that runs on its own origin, like Vite, Next.js or Flutter web.

docs.title: 1. Write the config
2. Set the origin per environment
docs.text:
CORS_ORIGIN is a new key. Add a getter for it to the AppEnv class:

lib/config/env.dart
  /// the front-end URL that may call the API
  String get corsOrigin => 'http://localhost:5173';

Run dart run build_runner build to update env.g.dart. Then set the value in .env:

.env
CORS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173

In staging and production, set CORS_ORIGIN as a real environment variable: https://my.app. The origin is scheme, host and port. No path, no / at the end.

docs.title: 3. Choose credentials
docs.text:
Your front-end sends origin credentials a token in Authorization: Bearer (see JWT authentication) your front-end URL false cookies (fetch(url, {credentials: 'include'})) your front-end URL, never * true nothing, a public API '*' false

Browsers do not send cookies when origin is *.

One origin only

Access-Control-Allow-Origin takes one origin or *. Dox sends the value of origin as it is. It does not compare it with the Origin header of the request. A list like ['https://a.com', 'https://b.com'] is joined to https://a.com,https://b.com. Browsers reject that. So set one origin per environment. For two front-ends, run two API hosts, or put a proxy in front that picks the header.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
The browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request before a POST with JSON or a custom header. Dox answers it by itself. You do not need an OPTIONS route.

curl -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:3000/api/users \
  -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization'

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:5173
access-control-allow-methods: GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE
access-control-allow-headers: Content-Type,Authorization
access-control-expose-headers: Content-Disposition
access-control-allow-credentials: false
access-control-max-age: 600

A normal request gets the origin header too:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/ping -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' | grep -i access-control-allow-origin

access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:5173

In the browser, open the front-end and call the API with fetch. The console shows no CORS error.

docs.title: When it still fails
docs.text: The console says The fix No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header CORS_ORIGIN does not match the page origin exactly. Check http or https, and the port. The value of ... header is 'a.com,b.com' More than one origin. Use one. Request header field x-foo is not allowed Add the header to headers. credentials mode is 'include' with * Set origin to the front-end URL and credentials: true.

docs.title: Webhooks and server-to-server calls
docs.text:
CORS only matters for browsers. A webhook from Stripe or a call from another server ignores these headers. Turn CORS off for such routes to send fewer headers:

Route.disabledCors(() {
  Route.post('/webhooks/stripe', webhookController.handle);
});

docs.text:
• CORS for every option
  • JWT authentication

docs.title: Custom errors
docs.text: Give your app its own exception classes, send every error in one JSON shape, and log the unexpected ones.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app.

docs.title: How Dox handles an error
docs.text:
When a controller or a middleware throws:

Error Status What Dox does an IHttpException, like NotFoundHttpException its code sends its message. Does not call errorHandler a validation error (bad DTO input) 422 sends the field errors. Does not call errorHandler any other Exception or Error 500 sends error.toString(). Calls errorHandler

The response goes through the responseHandler of AppConfig last. That is where you set the shape.

docs.title: 1. Write your own exceptions
docs.text:
Extend IHttpException. Set code (the HTTP status), errorCode (a short text for the client) and message.

lib/app/exceptions/app_exception.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// 403. Thrown when the user may not do this.
class ForbiddenException extends IHttpException {
  ForbiddenException({String message = 'Forbidden'}) {
    super.code = HttpStatus.forbidden;
    super.errorCode = 'forbidden';
    super.message = message;
  }
}

/// 409. Thrown when the row already exists or was changed by someone else.
class ConflictException extends IHttpException {
  ConflictException({String message = 'Conflict'}) {
    super.code = HttpStatus.conflict;
    super.errorCode = 'conflict';
    super.message = message;
  }
}

Throw them anywhere in a controller, a middleware or a service:

lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/exceptions/app_exception.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class UserController {
  /// GET /api/users/{id}
  Future<User> show(int id) async {
    User? user = await User().find(id);
    if (user == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'User $id not found');
    }
    return user;
  }

  /// DELETE /api/users/{id}
  Future<Map<String, bool>> destroy(int id) async {
    if (id == 1) {
      throw ForbiddenException(message: 'The first user can not be deleted');
    }
    User user = await show(id);
    await user.delete();
    return <String, bool>{'deleted': true};
  }
}

UserController userController = UserController();

docs.title: 2. One JSON shape for every error
docs.text:
The response handler sees every response before it is sent. For an error, the content is the exception object. Turn it into your shape here.

lib/app/http/response_handler.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Gives every error the same JSON shape:
/// `{"error": {"code": "not_found", "message": "..."}}`.
/// A validation error (422) also has `"errors": {field: message}`.
class ResponseHandler extends ResponseHandlerInterface {
  @override
  DoxResponse handle(DoxResponse res) {
    dynamic content = res.getContent();

    if (content is ValidationException) {
      return res.statusCode(content.code).content(<String, dynamic>{
        'error': <String, dynamic>{
          'code': content.errorCode,
          'message': 'The input is not valid',
        },
        'errors': content.message,
      });
    }

    if (content is IHttpException) {
      return res.statusCode(content.code).content(<String, dynamic>{
        'error': <String, dynamic>{
          'code': content.errorCode,
          'message': content.message.toString(),
        },
      });
    }

    // any other exception: hide the details from the client
    if (content is Exception || content is Error) {
      return res.statusCode(HttpStatus.internalServerError).content(
        <String, dynamic>{
          'error': <String, String>{
            'code': 'server_error',
            'message': 'Something went wrong',
          },
        },
      );
    }

    return res;
  }
}

The last if matters. Without it, a 500 sends error.toString() to the client. That can show a SQL query or a file path.

docs.title: 3. Log unexpected errors
docs.text:
errorHandler runs for every 500, and for errors outside a request (a future nobody awaited, a timer). Write one JSON line. A log collector reads it, or you send it to Sentry here.

lib/app/error_handler.dart
import 'dart:convert';

/// Dox calls this for every unexpected error (a `500`, or an error
/// outside a request). It does not run for `IHttpException` errors
/// like `404` or `422`, because those are expected.
/// One JSON line per error. Send it to Sentry or Datadog from here.
void reportError(Object? error, StackTrace stackTrace) {
  print(
    jsonEncode(<String, String>{
      'level': 'ERROR',
      'message': error.toString(),
      'stack': stackTrace.toString(),
      'timestamp': DateTime.now().toIso8601String(),
    }),
  );
}

docs.title: 4. Register both
Check it
docs.text:
Add a route that throws, only for this check:

Route.get('/boom', (DoxRequest req) => throw StateError('boom'));
Request Status Body GET /api/users/999 404 {"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"User 999 not found"}} GET /api/users/abc 404 {"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"Not Found"}} DELETE /api/users/1 403 {"error":{"code":"forbidden","message":"The first user can not be deleted"}} POST /api/auth/register with {} 422 {"error":{"code":"validation_failed","message":"The input is not valid"},"errors":{"name":"The name is required", ...}} GET /api/boom 500 {"error":{"code":"server_error","message":"Something went wrong"}}

After GET /api/boom, the server prints one line:

{"level":"ERROR","message":"Bad state: boom","stack":"#0  ApiRouter.register.<anonymous closure> (package:my_app/routes/api.dart:40:44) ...","timestamp":"2026-10-22T14:01:12.000Z"}

Remove the /boom route when you are done.

A URL with no route

A URL that matches no route answers 404 with the text GET /nothing not found. Dox answers this before the response handler runs, so it does not get the JSON shape. To change it, add a catch-all route at the end of your last router: Route.get('/{path*}', (DoxRequest req) => throw NotFoundHttpException()); Do the same for Route.post and the other methods you use.

docs.text:

  • Validation: the error response

docs.title: Deploy to Google Cloud Run
docs.text:
Run the blog API on Cloud Run from the Dockerfile of your project, with Postgres on Cloud SQL and secrets in Secret Manager.

Note

These steps follow the Cloud Run docs as of 2026-10-22 (checked on 2026-10-22). They were not run on Cloud Run in CI. The Docker image itself was built and run locally.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Google Cloud project with billing, and the gcloud CLI (gcloud auth login, gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID).
  • The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app, with the Dockerfile of a new Dox app. See Deployment: Docker for how that file works.
  • A Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance with a database and a user. See step 3.

The image is small. For the blog API it is about 17 MB.

Check for (native)

The project's Dockerfile copies libgcc_s.so.1 into the image, so the native HTTP server loads. The start log ends with (native). If it says using the dart:io server, see Docker.

docs.title: The port: PORT and APP_PORT
docs.text:
Cloud Run sends requests to one port of the container. It puts that port in the PORT env variable. The default is 8080.

Dox does not read PORT. It reads APP_PORT (default 3000), in lib/config/app.dart. So tell Cloud Run to use port 3000:

gcloud run deploy blog --port 3000 ...

Then Cloud Run sends requests to 3000 and sets PORT=3000. The app listens on 3000. No code change.

Or read PORT in the app

If you want the app to follow PORT, add a getter to lib/config/env.dart and use it in lib/config/app.dart, then run dart run build_runner build:

lib/config/env.dart
  /// set by Cloud Run
  int? get port;
lib/config/app.dart
serverPort: env.port ?? env.appPort,

Then you can leave out --port.

docs.title: 1. Turn on the APIs
docs.text:
gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com cloudbuild.googleapis.com \
  artifactregistry.googleapis.com secretmanager.googleapis.com sqladmin.googleapis.com

docs.title: 2. Save the secrets in Secret Manager
docs.text:
openssl rand -hex 16 | tr -d '\n' | gcloud secrets create blog-app-key --data-file=-
printf '%s' '<the database password>' | gcloud secrets create blog-db-password --data-file=-

Let the Cloud Run service account read them. By default this is the Compute Engine service account, PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com:

for s in blog-app-key blog-db-password; do
  gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding "$s" \
    --member="serviceAccount:PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com" \
    --role="roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor"
done

docs.title: 3. Reach Cloud SQL
docs.text:
Cloud Run has two ways to reach Cloud SQL: a Unix socket in /cloudsql/..., or the private IP over a VPC.

Dox connects to Postgres over TCP only. It can not use the Unix socket. So use the private IP:

  1. Give the Cloud SQL instance a private IP on your VPC network (for example default).
  2. Deploy the service with Direct VPC egress (--network, --subnet, --vpc-egress in step 4).
  3. Use the private IP as DB_HOST and 5432 as DB_PORT.

Do not use SQLite on Cloud Run. The file system of an instance is in memory, and each instance has its own. The data is lost when the instance stops.

docs.title: 4. Deploy from source
docs.text:
--source . uploads the folder. Cloud Build builds the image with your Dockerfile and saves it in Artifact Registry (in a repository named cloud-run-source-deploy).

gcloud run deploy blog \
  --source . \
  --region europe-west1 \
  --port 3000 \
  --allow-unauthenticated \
  --cpu 1 --memory 512Mi \
  --min-instances 1 \
  --network default --subnet default --vpc-egress private-ranges-only \
  --set-env-vars APP_ENV=production,APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE=1,DB_CONNECTION=postgres,DB_HOST=10.20.0.3,DB_PORT=5432,DB_NAME=blog,DB_USERNAME=blog \
  --set-secrets APP_KEY=blog-app-key:1,DB_PASSWORD=blog-db-password:1
Flag Why --port 3000 the port Dox listens on (APP_PORT). See the port --min-instances 1 keeps one instance warm, so the first request does not wait for a cold start. The default is 0. An idle instance still costs money --network, --subnet, --vpc-egress Direct VPC egress, to reach the private IP of Cloud SQL --set-env-vars config that is not secret --set-secrets ENV_NAME=SECRET:VERSION. Cloud Run reads the secret when an instance starts. Pin a version number, not latest APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE=1 one isolate per CPU. Set it to the --cpu value

To build the image yourself instead, push it to Artifact Registry and deploy it with --image:

docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/blog/api:1 .
docker push europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/blog/api:1
gcloud run deploy blog --image europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/blog/api:1 --region europe-west1 --port 3000 ...

Use the same other flags as above.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
gcloud run deploy prints the service URL at the end.

curl https://blog-xxxxxxxx-ew.a.run.app/api/ping

pong

gcloud run services logs read blog --region europe-west1 --limit 20
gcloud beta run services logs tail blog --region europe-west1   # live, needs the log-streaming component

The first log lines after a start:

Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
{"level":"INFO","name":"dox","message":"Server started at http://127.0.0.1:3000 with 1 isolate (native)", ...}

If the deploy fails with "the container did not listen on the port", the app listens on a different port than --port. Check APP_PORT and --port.

docs.title: HTTPS and the client IP
docs.text:
Cloud Run ends TLS and sends plain HTTP to the container. Only the Cloud Run front end can reach the container port. So ['*'] in trustedProxies is safe, and req.ip() and req.scheme() then show the real client:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  trustedProxies: <String>['*'],
);

See Deployment: HTTPS.

docs.title: Update the app
docs.text:
gcloud run deploy blog --source . --region europe-west1
  • Cloud Run keeps the flags of the last revision. You only pass what changes.
  • A new revision starts, runs new migrations, and takes the traffic when it listens on the port. The old one then stops.
  • When many instances start at the same time, each one runs the migrations. Keep migrations safe to run twice, or run one instance during a deploy with a migration.
  • A new secret version: create it with gcloud secrets versions add, then deploy with the new number in --update-secrets APP_KEY=blog-app-key:2.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Deployment for the bundle and the Dockerfile
  • Environments for all env keys and APP_KEY
  • Docker for a health check binary and Docker Compose
  • Cloud Run docs: container contract, deploy from source, secrets, minimum instances, Cloud SQL

docs.title: Deploy to Fly.io
docs.text:
Run the blog API on Fly.io from the Dockerfile of your project, with SQLite on a volume or with Postgres.

Note

These steps follow the Fly.io docs as of 2026-10-22 (checked on 2026-10-22). They were not run on Fly.io in CI. The Docker image itself was built and run locally.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Fly.io account and the fly CLI (fly auth login).
  • The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app, with the Dockerfile of a new Dox app. See Deployment: Docker for how that file works.

The image is small. For the blog API it is about 17 MB. Fly builds it for you on fly deploy.

Check for (native)

The project's Dockerfile copies libgcc_s.so.1 into the image, so the native HTTP server loads. The start log ends with (native). If it says using the dart:io server, see Docker.

docs.title: 1. Make the app on Fly.io
docs.text:
In the project folder:

fly launch --no-deploy

fly launch finds the Dockerfile, asks for an app name and a region, and writes fly.toml. --no-deploy stops before the first deploy, so you can set the config first.

docs.title: 2. Write fly.toml
docs.text:
Replace the file with this one. Change app and primary_region to your values.

fly.toml
app = "blog-api"
primary_region = "ams"

[build]
  dockerfile = "Dockerfile"

# config that is not secret. Secrets come from `fly secrets set`.
[env]
  APP_ENV = "production"
  APP_PORT = "3000"
  DB_CONNECTION = "sqlite"
  DB_NAME = "/data/blog.sqlite"

[http_service]
  internal_port = 3000
  force_https = true
  # one machine, always on: the SQLite file is on its volume
  auto_stop_machines = "off"
  auto_start_machines = true
  min_machines_running = 1

  [[http_service.checks]]
    grace_period = "10s"
    interval = "30s"
    method = "GET"
    timeout = "5s"
    path = "/api/ping"

# the volume with the SQLite file
[mounts]
  source = "blog_data"
  destination = "/data"

[[vm]]
  memory = "256mb"
  cpu_kind = "shared"
  cpus = 1
  • internal_port is the port the app listens on. Dox reads it from APP_PORT. Keep the two the same.
  • Values in [env] must be strings, so write "3000", not 3000.
  • [[vm]] wins over fly scale vm. Each fly deploy sets the machine to these values.

docs.title: 3. Set the secrets
docs.text:
fly secrets set APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>

A secret is an environment variable on every machine of the app. fly secrets list shows the names, not the values. A secret with the same name as an [env] key wins.

docs.title: SQLite on a volume
docs.text:
Make the volume that [mounts] asks for, in the same region:

fly volumes create blog_data --region ams --size 1
  • One volume is attached to one machine only. Fly.io does not copy the data between volumes.
  • So with SQLite, run exactly one machine.

docs.title: Postgres
docs.text:
Create a Fly.io Managed Postgres cluster with fly mpg create.

fly mpg attach sets one secret, DATABASE_URL. Dox does not read DATABASE_URL. It reads DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME, DB_USERNAME and DB_PASSWORD. So take the values from the connection string in the Managed Postgres dashboard, and set them yourself:

fly secrets set DB_CONNECTION=postgres \
  DB_HOST=<host> DB_PORT=5432 DB_NAME=<database> \
  DB_USERNAME=<user> DB_PASSWORD=<password>

Then delete DB_CONNECTION and DB_NAME from [env], and delete the [mounts] section. If the database asks for TLS, set useSSL: true on the postgres connection in lib/config/database.dart.

docs.title: 5. Deploy
docs.text:
fly deploy

fly deploy builds the image from the Dockerfile, makes the machine and starts it. The app runs the migrations at start.

Check that there is one machine:

fly scale show

If the count is more than 1 and you use SQLite, run fly scale count 1.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
curl https://blog-api.fly.dev/api/ping

pong

fly status    # the machines and their state
fly logs      # the app logs, live

The first log lines after a start:

Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
{"level":"INFO","name":"dox","message":"Server started at http://127.0.0.1:3000 with 1 isolate (native)", ...}

docs.title: HTTPS and the client IP
docs.text:
Fly.io ends TLS and sends plain HTTP to port 3000. force_https = true sends HTTP visitors to HTTPS. To make req.ip() and req.scheme() show the real client, set trustedProxies in AppConfig. The app port is reachable only through the Fly.io proxy, so ['*'] is safe here:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  trustedProxies: <String>['*'],
);

See Deployment: HTTPS.

docs.title: More CPU, more machines
docs.text:
Dox starts one isolate per CPU core it sees. On cpus = 1 that is one isolate.

You want Do this more speed on one machine raise cpus in [[vm]] (and memory), then fly deploy. Dox uses the new cores by itself more machines use Postgres, then fly scale count 2. With SQLite, stay at one machine a fixed number of isolates set APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE in [env]

Each machine is its own process. WebSocket rooms and the memory cache are not shared between machines.

docs.title: Update the app
docs.text:
fly deploy
  • Change config in [env] and run fly deploy again.
  • fly secrets set restarts the machines with the new value. With --stage it only saves the value, and the next deploy uses it.
  • The app runs new migrations at start.
  • With one machine there is a short gap while it restarts.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Deployment for the bundle and the Dockerfile
  • Environments for all env keys and APP_KEY
  • Docker for a health check binary and Docker Compose
  • Fly.io docs: fly.toml, secrets, volumes, Managed Postgres

docs.title: Deploy to a Linux server
docs.text:
Run the blog API on your own Linux server (a VPS), with systemd to keep it running and Caddy in front for HTTPS.

Note

These steps follow the systemd and Caddy docs as of 2026-10-22. They were not run on a real VPS in CI.

flowchart LR
  client[Browser or app] -- "HTTPS :443" --> caddy[Caddy]
  caddy -- "HTTP 127.0.0.1:3000" --> dox["/opt/blog/bin/server (systemd)"]

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Linux server (Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04 or newer) with SSH and sudo.
  • A domain name. Its A (and AAAA) record points to the server.
  • Docker on your machine, to build a Linux binary.
  • The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app.

docs.title: 1. Build the bundle for Linux
docs.text:
dox build makes a native binary for the system it runs on. A binary built on macOS does not run on Linux. So build it inside the dart:stable image (it is Debian):

docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/app -w /app dart:stable sh -c \
  'dart pub get && dart pub global activate dox 3.0.0-alpha.4 && /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build'

The result is build/bundle/:

build/bundle/
  bin/server                         the AOT binary
  lib/dox_http_native-linux-*.so     the native HTTP server
  lib/libsqlite3.so                  SQLite
  db/                                the migrations
  .env.example

The container shares your project folder. It writes Linux paths into .dart_tool/. So run dart pub get on your machine again before you use dox serve.

Keep bin/ and lib/ together. The binary loads the libraries from ../lib. See Deployment for more about the bundle.

Match the CPU of the server

Docker builds for the CPU of your machine. On a Mac with Apple silicon that is arm64. Most VPS plans are x86_64. For them, add --platform linux/amd64 after docker run. Check the server with uname -m.

docs.title: 2. Make a user and the folders
docs.text:
Run this on the server. The app runs as the user dox. This user can not log in.

sudo useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin dox
sudo mkdir -p /opt/blog
sudo install -d -o dox -g dox /opt/blog/storage
Path What it holds Owner /opt/blog the bundle (bin/, lib/, db/) root /opt/blog/storage files the app writes (uploads, file cache) dox /var/lib/blog the SQLite file. systemd makes it (see step 5) dox /etc/blog.env config and secrets root, mode 600

docs.title: 3. Copy the bundle to the server
docs.text:
rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ build/bundle/ you@server:/tmp/blog-bundle/
ssh you@server 'sudo rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ /tmp/blog-bundle/ /opt/blog/'

docs.title: 4. Write the env file
docs.text:
/etc/blog.env
APP_NAME=blog
APP_ENV=production
APP_PORT=3000
APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>

DB_CONNECTION=sqlite
DB_NAME=/var/lib/blog/blog.sqlite

sudo chown root:root /etc/blog.env
sudo chmod 600 /etc/blog.env

systemd reads this file as root, before it starts the app as dox. So dox does not need to read it.

For Postgres, set DB_CONNECTION=postgres and add DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD and DB_NAME. See Environments for all keys.

Which value wins

Env.get() reads a real environment variable first. It reads the .env file in the working folder only when the variable is not set. systemd gives the app the lines of EnvironmentFile as real environment variables. So /etc/blog.env wins over a /opt/blog/.env. Do not put a .env in /opt/blog, so there is only one place to look.

docs.title: 5. Write the systemd unit
docs.text:
/etc/systemd/system/blog.service
[Unit]
Description=Blog API (Dox)
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=dox
Group=dox
# the binary reads db/ and .env from this folder
WorkingDirectory=/opt/blog
EnvironmentFile=/etc/blog.env
ExecStart=/opt/blog/bin/server
# start again after a crash, and after `kill`
Restart=always
RestartSec=2
# makes /var/lib/blog, owned by the user dox
StateDirectory=blog
# small safety settings
NoNewPrivileges=true
PrivateTmp=true
ProtectSystem=full

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now blog
systemctl status blog
  • Restart=always: when the main isolate dies, the process exits and systemd starts it again. See Deployment: keep it running.
  • The app runs the migrations at start, before it takes requests.
  • Dox starts one isolate per CPU core. Set APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE in /etc/blog.env to change it.

docs.title: 6. Close the app port
docs.text:
Dox listens on all network interfaces. It has no option to listen on 127.0.0.1 only. So block port 3000 from outside with a firewall. Only Caddy should reach it.

sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable

docs.title: 7. Put Caddy in front
docs.text:
Install Caddy from its install page. The Debian package runs Caddy with systemd and reads /etc/caddy/Caddyfile.

/etc/caddy/Caddyfile
api.example.com {
    encode zstd gzip

    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000 {
        # while the app restarts, wait up to 10s for it instead of failing
        lb_try_duration 10s
        lb_try_interval 250ms
    }
}

sudo caddy validate --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile
sudo systemctl reload caddy
  • Caddy gets a TLS certificate for api.example.com by itself. Ports 80 and 443 must be open.
  • reverse_proxy sets X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto.

docs.title: 8. Trust Caddy in the app
docs.text:
Dox ignores X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto until you list the proxy in trustedProxies. Caddy talks to the app from the same server:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1'],
);

Now req.ip() is the real client IP and req.scheme() is https. Build and copy again after this change (steps 1 and 3). See Deployment: HTTPS.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
curl https://api.example.com/api/ping

pong

Read the logs. In production the app writes one JSON line per log.

journalctl -u blog -f                     # follow new lines
journalctl -u blog --since "1 hour ago"   # the last hour
journalctl -u blog -b                     # since the last boot

The first lines after a start look like this:

Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
{"level":"INFO","name":"dox","message":"Server started at http://127.0.0.1:3000 with 2 isolate (native)", ...}

(native) means the native HTTP server loaded. (dart:io) means it did not, and the line before it says why.

Check that the app port is closed. From your machine:

curl -m 5 http://api.example.com:3000/api/ping   # must time out

docs.title: Update the app
docs.text:
1. Build a new bundle (step 1).

  2. Copy it to the server (step 3). Keep the old one first, so you can go back:

    ssh you@server 'sudo rm -rf /opt/blog.prev && sudo cp -a /opt/blog /opt/blog.prev'
rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ build/bundle/ you@server:/tmp/blog-bundle/
ssh you@server 'sudo rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ /tmp/blog-bundle/ /opt/blog/'

  3. Restart the app. It runs new migrations at start.

    ssh you@server 'sudo systemctl restart blog'

  4. Read the logs (journalctl -u blog -n 20) and run the check.

To go back: copy /opt/blog.prev to /opt/blog and restart. A migration that already ran is not undone.

A restart is short, but not zero

A restart takes about one second. Dox does not wait for open requests when it stops, so a request that is running at that moment fails. New requests do not fail: lb_try_duration makes Caddy wait for the app to come back. For a real zero-downtime update, run two copies on two ports and list both in Caddy. See Deployment: many processes.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Deployment for dox build, Docker, nginx and many processes
  • Environments for config per environment and APP_KEY
  • Docker to run the app and Postgres with Docker Compose
  • Native server

docs.title: Docker
docs.text: Build a small production image with dox build, and run it with Postgres in Docker Compose, with a health check.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app with a database.
  • Docker with Compose.

docs.title: 1. Add a health route
docs.text:
The health check asks this route. It fails when the database does not answer.

lib/app/http/controllers/health.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

class HealthController {
  /// GET /health. 200 when the app and the database answer.
  /// Any database error becomes a 500, so the health check fails.
  Future<Map<String, String>> check(DoxRequest req) async {
    await QueryBuilder.query('select 1');
    return <String, String>{'status': 'ok'};
  }
}

HealthController healthController = HealthController();
lib/routes/web.dart
Route.get('/health', healthController.check);

docs.title: 2. Add the health check binary
docs.text:
The final image is FROM scratch. It has no shell and no curl. So the health check is a second small Dart binary.

bin/health.dart
import 'dart:io';

/// Docker health check. The final image has no shell and no curl,
/// so this small binary asks the app itself. Exit 0 = healthy.
Future<void> main() async {
  String port = Platform.environment['APP_PORT'] ?? '3000';
  HttpClient client = HttpClient()
    ..connectionTimeout = const Duration(seconds: 3);
  try {
    HttpClientRequest request = await client.getUrl(
      Uri.parse('http://127.0.0.1:$port/health'),
    );
    HttpClientResponse response = await request.close();
    exit(response.statusCode == 200 ? 0 : 1);
  } catch (_) {
    exit(1);
  }
}

docs.title: 3. Write the Dockerfile
docs.text:
Two stages. The first one has the Dart SDK and the dox CLI, and builds the AOT bundle. The second one has only the Dart runtime files and the bundle. No SDK, no source, no shell.

Dockerfile
# Stage 1: build the AOT bundle with the Dart SDK and the dox CLI.
FROM dart:stable AS build

WORKDIR /app

# Resolve dependencies first, so Docker caches this layer.
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get

COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline

# `dox build` runs build_runner, then `dart build cli`.
# The bundle is in build/bundle: bin/server, lib/, db/, .env.example
RUN dart pub global activate dox 3.0.0-alpha.4 \
  && /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build

# The health check binary. Plain dart:io, so `dart compile exe` is fine.
RUN dart compile exe bin/health.dart -o build/bundle/bin/health

# Lay out the final file tree. /tmp must be writable: uploads bigger
# than 1 MB are streamed to a temp file.
RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/app/public /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ \
  && cp -r public/. /out/app/public/ \
  # the native HTTP server (Rust) needs libgcc_s, which /runtime/ does not have
  && LIBGCC=$(find / -name libgcc_s.so.1 -path '*lib*' | head -n 1) \
  && mkdir -p /out$(dirname $LIBGCC) && cp $LIBGCC /out$LIBGCC

# Stage 2: the Dart AOT runtime and the bundle only. No SDK, no source.
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app

# Config comes from env variables. The image has no .env file.
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s --timeout=5s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \
  CMD ["/app/bin/health"]
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]

Delete the public lines when your app has no public folder.

Check the start log in the container. It must end with (native):

Server started at http://127.0.0.1:3000 with 8 isolate (native)

Without the libgcc_s lines, the native HTTP server does not load in a scratch image. Dox then prints dox_http_native did not load, using the dart:io server and runs on the slower dart:io server.

dox build, not dart compile exe

dox_orm bundles SQLite with a build hook. dart compile exe does not run build hooks and stops with an error. dox build runs dart build cli, which does. It puts the native libraries in build/bundle/lib, next to bin/server.

Keep the build context small:

.dockerignore
.dart_tool/
.git/
.github/
.idea/
build/
storage/
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
Dockerfile
docker-compose.yml
pubspec_overrides.yaml

docs.title: 4. Write the compose file
docs.text:
The app reads its config from env variables. env_file: .env gives it your .env. The lines under environment win over the file, so the app always talks to the postgres service.

docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    # secrets and config come from .env, never from the image
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      APP_ENV: production
      APP_PORT: 3000
      DB_CONNECTION: postgres
      DB_HOST: postgres
      DB_PORT: 5432
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    volumes:
      # uploads survive a new image
      - uploads:/app/storage
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped

  postgres:
    image: postgres:18
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USERNAME:-postgres}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:?set DB_PASSWORD in .env}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_NAME:-dox}
    volumes:
      - postgres:/var/lib/postgresql
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-q", "-U", "${DB_USERNAME:-postgres}"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  postgres:
  uploads:
  • depends_on with service_healthy: the app starts after Postgres answers. The app runs the migrations at start, so the database must be up.
  • ${DB_PASSWORD:?...}: compose stops with a clear message when .env has no password.
  • restart: unless-stopped: when the main isolate dies, the process exits and Docker starts it again.

docs.title: 5. Write the .env
docs.text:
.env
APP_NAME=my_app
APP_ENV=production
APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>
APP_PORT=3000

DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_NAME=my_app
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=<a real password>

.env is in .dockerignore and .gitignore. It never goes into the image or into git.

docs.title: 6. Build and run
docs.text:
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose ps

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
docker compose ps

NAME             STATUS
my_app-app-1       Up 30 seconds (healthy)
my_app-postgres-1  Up 35 seconds (healthy)

curl http://localhost:3000/health

{"status":"ok"}

Stop Postgres with docker compose stop postgres. After about 45 seconds, docker compose ps shows the app as unhealthy.

docs.title: HTTPS
docs.text: Do not add TLS to the app. Put Caddy or nginx in front, and set trustedProxies in AppConfig. See Deployment: HTTPS.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Deployment for dox build, the bundle layout and systemd
  • Environments for dev, staging and production config
  • Migration: run on server start

docs.title: Environments
docs.text: Run the same app in development, staging and production with different config, and keep secrets out of git and out of the image.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app.
  • build_runner for the typed env class (a new app has it).

docs.title: How Dox reads config
docs.text:
1. A real environment variable (shell, Docker, systemd) wins.
  2. Then the .env file in the folder where the app starts.

So: use .env on your machine. Use real environment variables on a server. The .env file is optional there.

docs.title: 1. The typed env class
docs.text:
A new project already has lib/config/env.dart. Its AppEnv class lists every key, its type and its default. A missing required key stops the app at start, with a list of all problems.

This is the file of the guides app. The last two getters, corsOrigin and appUrl, are keys this app added. The rest comes with a new project.

lib/config/env.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'env.g.dart';

/// The env of the app, typed. Made by `dox env:generate`.
/// -------------------------------
/// Each getter reads one key: `appName` reads `APP_NAME`.
/// A getter body is the default. A nullable getter is optional.
/// Other getters are required: the app stops at startup when one is missing.
/// Run `dart run build_runner build` after you change this class.
@DoxEnv()
abstract class AppEnv {
  /// reads and checks every key once
  static AppEnv load([EnvReader? reader]) {
    return _$AppEnv.load(reader);
  }

  String get appName => 'dox';

  /// development, staging or production
  String get appEnv => 'development';

  bool get isDevelopment => appEnv == 'development';

  int get appPort => 3000;

  /// required: used to sign tokens and encrypt cookies
  String get appKey;

  /// isolates (threads) of the HTTP server. Null: one per CPU core.
  int? get appTotalIsolate;

  String get logLevel => 'info';

  /// memory, file or redis
  String get cacheStore => 'file';

  /// local, s3 or memory
  String get storageDisk => 'local';

  /// sqlite, postgres or mysql
  String get dbConnection => 'sqlite';

  /// the database name. For SQLite: the file path.
  String get dbName => 'db/dox.sqlite';

  String get dbHost => 'localhost';

  /// null: 5432 for Postgres, 3306 for MySQL
  int? get dbPort;

  String get dbUsername => 'postgres';

  String get dbPassword => '';

  /// the front-end URL that may call the API
  String get corsOrigin => 'http://localhost:5173';

  /// the public URL of this app, used in file links
  String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:3000';
}

/// The env of the app. Read and checked once, on first use.
final AppEnv env = AppEnv.load();

The key is the getter name in UPPER_SNAKE case: dbPort reads DB_PORT.

  • A getter with a body has a default: int get appPort => 3000;.
  • A nullable getter with no body is optional: int? get dbPort; is null when the key is not set.
  • Any other getter with no body is required: String get appKey;.

The part file env.g.dart is made by build_runner. It is in .gitignore.

docs.title: 2. Add a key
docs.text:
Say the app needs a mail host. Add one getter to AppEnv:

  /// the SMTP server for mails
  String get mailHost => 'localhost';

Then run build_runner again:

dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs

Now env.mailHost reads MAIL_HOST. Add MAIL_HOST to .env.example too.

docs.title: 3. Use it in the config files
docs.text:
The config files read the typed getters. Things that differ per environment become one if or one bool.

lib/config/logger.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

LoggerConfig logger = LoggerConfig(
  name: env.appName,
  enabled: true,
  level: env.logLevel,
  // colors on your machine, one JSON line per log in staging and production
  prettyPrint: env.isDevelopment,
);
lib/config/database.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 5432,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      // print every query on your machine only
      debug: env.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: env.dbName,
      debug: env.isDevelopment,
    ),
  },
);

docs.title: 4. Write the env files
docs.text:
Commit .env.example. It lists every key with a safe value. Never commit .env.

.env.example
APP_NAME=my_app
APP_ENV=development
APP_PORT=3000
# run `dox key:generate`
APP_KEY=
APP_URL=http://localhost:3000

DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=my_app
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=postgres

CORS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173
LOG_LEVEL=debug

cp .env.example .env
dox key:generate   # writes a new APP_KEY into .env
.gitignore
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
Environment Where the values live APP_ENV your machine .env development staging real env variables (compose environment:, a secrets manager) staging production real env variables production

On a server you can also keep a .env next to the binary, outside git, with chmod 600. systemd reads it with EnvironmentFile=. See Deployment.

docs.title: 5. APP_KEY
docs.text:
APP_KEY encrypts cookies and signs JWT tokens and local signed URLs.

  • Make one per environment with dox key:generate. Never share the production key with staging.
  • When APP_ENV=production and APP_KEY is empty, the app does not start.
  • A new key makes every cookie, token and signed URL invalid. Every user is logged out. Plan it.

docs.title: 6. Check the env before a deploy
docs.text:
dox env:check loads AppEnv with the real environment and .env, and prints every missing or bad key. It exits with code 1, so CI stops.

dox env:check

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Start with a key missing:

APP_KEY= dart run bin/server.dart

Unhandled exception:
EnvException: the env is not valid
  - APP_KEY is missing

Start as staging on another port. The real variables win over .env:

APP_ENV=staging APP_PORT=4000 dart run bin/server.dart

The app listens on 4000. env.appEnv is 'staging', and env.isDevelopment is false.

docs.title: Things that differ per environment
docs.text: Setting Development Staging and production prettyPrint of the logger true false (one JSON line per log) debug of the database true false totalIsolate 1 or 2 is enough one per core (the default) CORS_ORIGIN http://localhost:5173 the real front-end URL the server dox serve (JIT) the dox build binary (AOT)

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Environment variables for all types and rules of the typed env class
  • Docker
  • Deployment

docs.title: File upload
docs.text: Accept an image from a form, check its size and type, save it to a disk, and return its URL.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app (dox create my_app).
  • build_runner for the DTO (a new app has it).

docs.title: 1. Set up the disk
docs.text:
Give the local disk a url. Storage().url() uses it to build the public URL of a file.

lib/config/storage.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

StorageConfig storage = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    /// uploads go to the `storage` folder.
    /// `url` is the public address of `Route.files('files', ...)`.
    'local': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'local',
      'root': 'storage',
      'url': '${env.appUrl}/files',
    },
  },
);

APP_URL is a new key. Add a getter for it to the AppEnv class:

lib/config/env.dart
  /// the public URL of this app, used in file links
  String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:3000';

Run dart run build_runner build to update env.g.dart. Then add APP_URL=http://localhost:3000 to your .env.

docs.title: 2. Write the DTO
docs.text:
The DTO checks the file before your controller runs. @Image() reads the first bytes of the file to find the real type. It does not trust the file name.

lib/app/http/dtos/upload_image.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'upload_image.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class UploadImage {
  /// jpg, jpeg, png, gif, webp or bmp. Dox reads the first bytes of the
  /// file to find the real type. The file name is not trusted.
  @Image()
  @MaxSize('5MB')
  final RequestFile image;

  const UploadImage({required this.image});

  static const DtoSchema<UploadImage> schema = $UploadImageDto;
}

For other file types, use @Mimes(<String>['pdf', 'docx']) in place of @Image().

docs.title: 3. Write the controller
docs.text:
putRequestFile moves the upload to the disk with a new UUID name. It does not read the file into memory.

lib/app/http/controllers/upload.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/dtos/upload_image.dto.dart';

class UploadController {
  /// POST /api/upload (multipart/form-data, field `image`)
  Future<Map<String, String>> store(UploadImage body) async {
    // saves the file as /images/<uuid>.<ext> on the default disk
    String path = await Storage().putRequestFile('images', body.image);
    String url = await Storage().url(path);
    return <String, String>{'path': path, 'url': url};
  }
}

UploadController uploadController = UploadController();

Save the file before you return

A file bigger than 1 MB is written to a temp file while it arrives. Dox deletes that temp file when the response is sent. So call putRequestFile, store or moveTo inside the controller, not later.

docs.title: 4. Add the routes
docs.text:
One route takes the upload. Route.files serves the saved files at GET /files/{key*}.

lib/routes/api.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/upload.controller.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.post('/upload', uploadController.store);
  }
}
lib/routes/web.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    // GET /files/{key*}, any file of the default disk
    Route.files('files', signed: false);
  }
}

signed: false makes every file public. Leave it out to serve only signed URLs. Then use Storage().signedUrl(path) in place of Storage().url(path).

docs.title: 5. Build and run
docs.text:
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

Make sure lib/config/app.dart has dtos: dtos from lib/dtos.g.dart. See Validation: setup.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Upload a PNG:

curl -F image=@photo.png http://localhost:3000/api/upload

{"path":"/images/074aa0d0-ce21-11f1-938a-57265e28c4a3.png","url":"http://localhost:3000/files/images/074aa0d0-ce21-11f1-938a-57265e28c4a3.png"}

Open the url in the browser. The image shows.

Upload a text file. You get 422:

curl -F image=@notes.txt http://localhost:3000/api/upload

{"image":"The image must be an image"}

Send no file at all. You get 422 with {"image":"The image is required"}.

docs.title: Bigger files
docs.text: The default limit for a multipart/form-data body is 100 MB. Change it in AppConfig(maxMultipartSize: ...). Set the same limit in your proxy (client_max_body_size in nginx).

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Request: form data for RequestFile
  • Validation: files for @Image, @Mimes, @MaxSize
  • File storage for S3 and signed URLs

docs.title: JWT authentication
docs.text: Let users register and log in, give them a JWT token, protect routes with it, and read the user in a controller.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app with a database and a users table with name, email and password columns.
  • The dox_auth package: dart pub add dox_auth. A new app has it.
  • build_runner for the DTOs.

docs.title: 1. Hide the password in the model
docs.text:
The token holds user.toJson(). Anyone with the token can read it. So the password hash must be in hidden.

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'users', softDelete: true)
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password'];

  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? email;

  @Column()
  String? password;
}

docs.title: 2. Set up the auth service
docs.text:
APP_KEY signs the tokens. expiresIn is how long a token works.

lib/services/auth_service.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

class AuthService implements DoxService {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(
      AuthConfig(
        defaultGuard: 'api',
        guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
          'api': AuthGuard(
            driver: JwtAuthDriver(
              // APP_KEY signs the tokens. A new key logs every user out.
              secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
              // a token stops working after this time
              expiresIn: const Duration(days: 7),
            ),
            provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
          ),
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}
lib/config/services.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/services/auth_service.dart';
import 'package:my_app/services/orm_service.dart';

List<DoxService> services = <DoxService>[
  ORMService(),
  AuthService(),
];

docs.title: 3. Write the DTOs
docs.text:
@Unique makes sure the email is not taken. It comes from dox_orm, so hide its Schema class.

lib/app/http/dtos/register_user.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart' hide Schema;

part 'register_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class RegisterUser {
  @Length(min: 2, max: 50)
  @Trim()
  final String name;

  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  @Unique('users', column: 'email')
  final String email;

  @MinLength(8)
  final String password;

  const RegisterUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<RegisterUser> schema = $RegisterUserDto;
}
lib/app/http/dtos/login_user.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'login_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class LoginUser {
  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  final String email;

  final String password;

  const LoginUser({required this.email, required this.password});

  static const DtoSchema<LoginUser> schema = $LoginUserDto;
}

docs.title: 4. Write the controller
5. Add the routes
docs.text:
AuthMiddleware reads the Authorization: Bearer <token> header, checks the token and loads the user from the database. A missing or bad token stops the request with 401.

lib/routes/api.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.post('/auth/register', authController.register);
    Route.post('/auth/login', authController.login);

    Route.middleware(<dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()], () {
      Route.get('/auth/me', authController.me);
      Route.post('/auth/logout', authController.logout);
      // put every protected route here
    });
  }
}

docs.title: 6. Build and run
docs.text:
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Register:

curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}' \
  http://localhost:3000/api/auth/register

{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...","user":{"id":1,"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","created_at":"...","updated_at":"..."}}

Log in with a wrong password. You get 401:

{"error":{"code":"unauthorized","message":"Wrong email or password"}}

Log in and use the token:

TOKEN=$(curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}' \
  http://localhost:3000/api/auth/login | jq -r .token)

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://localhost:3000/api/auth/me

{"id":1,"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","created_at":"...","updated_at":"..."}

Without the header, /api/auth/me gives 401 Authentication failed.

The error shape

The 401 body above is the plain message of the exception. With the response handler from Custom errors, it becomes {"error":{"code":"unauthorized","message":"..."}}.

docs.title: Logout and expiry
docs.text:
A JWT is checked by its signature, not by a list on the server. So the server can not cancel one token. This is what you can do:

You want Do this Log out on this device The client deletes the token. That is all logout does. Limit the damage of a stolen token Keep expiresIn short, for example Duration(hours: 12). Log every user out at once Change APP_KEY. Every old token stops working. Block one user Delete or disable the user. AuthMiddleware loads the user from the database on each request, so a deleted user gets 401.

For a real "log out everywhere" button, add a token_version column to users, put it in the token, and compare the two in a middleware after AuthMiddleware.

docs.text:

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text: Make a list route that takes page and per_page from the query string and returns one page of rows.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app with a database and a User model (dox create:model User -m).
  • build_runner for the DTO.

docs.title: 1. Write the query DTO
docs.text:
A DTO with source: Source.query reads the query string, also for POST. The query key of perPage is per_page, because keys are snake_case by default.

lib/app/http/dtos/list_users.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'list_users.dto.g.dart';

/// GET /api/users?page=2&per_page=10
@Dto(source: Source.query)
class ListUsers {
  @Min(1)
  final int page;

  @Range(1, 100)
  final int perPage; // query key: per_page

  const ListUsers({this.page = 1, this.perPage = 20});

  static const DtoSchema<ListUsers> schema = $ListUsersDto;
}

Both fields have a default, so both are optional. @Range(1, 100) stops a client from asking for 10000 rows.

docs.title: 2. Write the controller
docs.text:
paginate() runs one count query and one select query. It returns a Pagination. A controller can return it as it is. Dox sends toJson().

lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/dtos/list_users.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class UserController {
  /// GET /api/users?page=1&per_page=20
  Future<Pagination> index(ListUsers query) async {
    return User()
        .orderBy('id', 'desc')
        .paginate(currentPage: query.page, perPage: query.perPage);
  }
}

UserController userController = UserController();

Always add an orderBy. Without it, the database may return the rows in a different order on each page.

Add a where before paginate to filter: User().where('role', 'admin').orderBy('id').paginate(...).

docs.title: 3. Add the route
docs.text:
lib/routes/api.dart
Route.get('/users', userController.index);

docs.title: 4. Build and run
docs.text:
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
With 3 users in the table:

curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/users?page=2&per_page=2'

{
  "total": 3,
  "per_page": 2,
  "last_page": 2,
  "current_page": 2,
  "data": [
    {"id": 1, "name": "User 1", "email": "user1@example.com", "created_at": "2026-10-22T14:01:07.843207Z", "updated_at": "2026-10-22T14:01:07.843207Z"}
  ]
}
Key Meaning total rows that match the query, on all pages per_page rows per page last_page the number of the last page current_page the page you asked for data the rows of this page, from toJson() of the model

A page after the last one gives an empty data list.

Bad input gets 422 before the controller runs:

curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/users?page=0&per_page=500'

{"page":"The page must be greater than or equal 1","per_page":"The per_page must be between 1 and 100"}

docs.title: Change the shape of a row
docs.text:
Return a serializer for each row, when the model has fields you do not want to send. page.getData<User>() gives the typed rows:

Future<Map<String, dynamic>> index(ListUsers query) async {
  Pagination page = await User()
      .orderBy('id', 'desc')
      .paginate(currentPage: query.page, perPage: query.perPage);
  return <String, dynamic>{
    ...page.toJson(),
    'data': UserSerializer(page.getData<User>()).toJson(),
  };
}

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Query builder: paginate
  • Validation: where the data comes from
  • Serializer

docs.title: Share code with Flutter
docs.text:
